docs.title: Use it from
docs.text:
One knowledge store, every surface: each calls the same Guru methods and the same tools, so an agent sees the same view wherever it runs.

Python MCP CLI LangChain / LlamaIndex / OpenAI Agents HTTP server 
import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")  # crawls the catalog: metadata only
guru.measure(all=True)                                # what the data says: joins, values, nulls
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")                 # what people know, in reviewable YAML
print(guru.context("monthly revenue by customer segment").text)

refused = guru.find_path("shop.orders", "shop.events")
print(refused.refusal, "-", refused.explanation)      # a route through a hub is refused
guru.close()

This block runs as written in the docs test, on the shop warehouse. More in Getting started.

pip install 'schemaguru[mcp,duckdb]'
schemaguru --url duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb --store .schemaguru/shop.db mcp

Serves the tools, plus a schema://tables/{ref} resource per table, over stdio. Client configuration: Agents, tools and MCP.

pip install 'schemaguru[duckdb]'
export SCHEMAGURU_URL=duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb
schemaguru crawl
schemaguru measure --all
schemaguru context "monthly revenue by customer segment"
schemaguru path shop.orders shop.events    # exit 1: the route pivots through a hub

Every command: CLI reference.

from schemaguru.agent.adapters import langchain as sg_langchain

tools = sg_langchain.tools(guru)            # StructuredTools; results are JSON text
agent_model = chat_model.bind_tools(tools)
retriever = sg_langchain.retriever(guru, k=4)   # describe_table documents per hit

from schemaguru.agent.adapters import llamaindex as sg_llamaindex

tools = sg_llamaindex.tool_spec(guru)       # FunctionTools

from agents import Agent

from schemaguru.agent.adapters import openai_agents as sg_openai

agent = Agent(name="analyst", instructions=guru.prompt_block(),
              tools=sg_openai.function_tools(guru))

One extra each (langchain, llamaindex, openai-agents). See Framework adapters.

pip install 'schemaguru[server,duckdb]'
export SCHEMAGURU_SERVER_TOKENS="$READER_TOKEN:reader"
schemaguru --url duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb --store .schemaguru/shop.db serve --port 8080

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/context \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $READER_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "monthly revenue by customer segment"}'

Routes, roles and a shared Postgres store: Server mode.

docs.text:
Runnable, offline examples live in the repository's examples/ folder. Each builds the shop warehouse on first run (from a repository checkout) or takes a DuckDB file as its first argument; the docs test runs every one of them.

Example Shows Needs duckdb_quickstart.py connect, view before and after measuring, an overlay, a safe and a refused join path schemaguru[duckdb] langchain_agent.py the LangChain tools in a tool-calling loop driven by a scripted stand-in model, and the retriever schemaguru[duckdb,langchain] anthropic_tools.py the tools= list for the Anthropic SDK and answering tool_use blocks with run_tool_use (no SDK, no network) schemaguru[duckdb] large_table_sampling.py the sampling decision for a 2 TiB table, and how sampled numbers render (≈, intervals, lower bounds) schemaguru[duckdb] mcp_server.md serving the tools over MCP and configuring a client schemaguru[mcp] schemaguru.yaml the example overlay the others load —

The examples measure through FactLang (0.1.4 or later, installed with SchemaGuru). docs.title: Features
docs.text:
What works out of the box in 0.2.1 (alpha). Each card links to its guide. Try it first in the playground or read the landing page for the short version.

Readers

The ClickHouse, DuckDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Trino readers are tested against real engines in CI. The BigQuery, Databricks, Oracle, Redshift and Snowflake readers are built from the documented system views and tested on recorded metadata, not yet validated against live accounts. Azure Synapse is supported through the SQL Server reader and is not tested in CI.

docs.title: Why it matters: a wrong guess does not error
docs.text: An agent that writes SQL against a warehouse knows what the names tell it. Names mislead in at least three common ways, and each returns a plausible, wrong number instead of an error. These three come from the shop warehouse SchemaGuru is tested on; the row counts are counted with plain SQL on that warehouse.

docs.title: 1. The wrong join
docs.text:
An agent asked for events per order joins orders → accounts → events on account_id. Both joins are "correct" (match rate 100%), yet the result has 3,335,000 rows for 10,000 orders — 333.5× — because both tables attribute many rows to one account. No error, a plausible number.

SchemaGuru measured both joins, saw accounts receiving two attribution edges, and refuses the route (find_join_path / schemaguru path shop.orders shop.events):

every route shop.orders -> shop.events pivots through hub shop.accounts on two attribution edges (fan-in > 10): a cartesian hazard

A safe route is returned with its keys and its weakest support:

  shop.payments → shop.orders → shop.customers · support 98.04%
    payments.order_id = orders.order_id (1:1)
    orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id (N:1)

docs.title: 2. The soft-delete flag that is never FALSE
docs.text:
orders.deleted is TRUE or NULL — never FALSE. The filter an agent writes from the name, WHERE NOT deleted, returns 0 rows; the live rows are 9,700. The measured values sit next to the human's soft-delete rule:

  live rows: (deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted) (human, unchecked)
    deleted      BOOLEAN  values: TRUE (300) (measured 2026-11-24); null 97% (measured 2026-11-24); distinct 1 (measured 2026-11-24)

docs.title: 3. The enum that drifted in case
docs.text:
WHERE status = 'paid' counts 5,000 orders; 5,412 are paid. The overlay declares paid, refunded, cancelled; measurement found PAID as well. SchemaGuru keeps the human expectation and states the contradiction (here under a waiver with an expiry date):

  ⚠ WAIVED until 2027-01-31 (legacy upper-case rows being migrated): status: declared values 'paid','refunded','cancelled' — observed also 'PAID' (412 rows)
  ⚠ status: case drift: 'paid'/'PAID' differ only in case — compare case-insensitively
    status       VARCHAR  values: 'paid','refunded','cancelled' (+ observed 'PAID'); distinct 4 (measured 2026-11-24); Payment state of the order.

docs.title: How SchemaGuru catches them
docs.text:
Trap What SchemaGuru does Read more Row-multiplying join measures every candidate join in both directions (match rate, reverse coverage, fan-in); refuses a route that arrives at a hub on one many-to-one edge and leaves on another (HUB_PIVOT) Join graph TRUE/NULL flag measures observed values and the null rate; shows the human's live-rows predicate next to them Measure Case drift keeps a declared enum as an expectation, never rewrites it; reports what measurement saw beyond it Overlays Narrow join a thin but correct join is returned labelled with its coverage; only broken joins are refused Join graph Stale knowledge refresh re-measures, diffs against the previous snapshot and classifies each change Refresh

Every statement carries its provenance (catalog, declared, measured, drafted by an LLM, or human) and every measured number carries its method and date. Unknown is shown as unknown, never as 0 or 100%. A view that shows a warning also says that the absence of a warning is not verification.

docs.title: Where it shines
docs.text:
Agents on huge warehouses. Metadata-only, paged, resumable crawls; search runs in the store's full-text index, so a view is scoped without loading every table. Lazy, budgeted measurement: an agent's question never spends warehouse money by itself.

Onboarding analysts. schemaguru context "<question>" prints what a newcomer needs: which tables answer it, which joins are measured, which columns hold traps.

Data-contract CI. Declare enums, joins and soft-delete rules in YAML; schemaguru refresh exits 1 when a change needs review, and view fingerprints detect prompt drift.

Migration audits. Measure the same joins before and after a move; the refresh report says which verdicts changed, judged relative to the previous snapshot.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
Measured on the developer's machine (hardware-dependent): lexical table search over a synthetic 500,000-table store and graph expansion over 50,000 joins are fast; the whole context call at that size is not.

At 500,000 tables the context call has a p95 of 28.6 s, which misses its 200 ms target; this is a known limit, see Scale.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
SchemaGuru architecture The warehouse feeds catalog readers, which write to the store. Measurement with FactLang, human YAML overlays and lineage also write to the store. The join graph and question scoping read the store, rendering turns the scoped result into a view, and agents receive it as a prompt, tools, an MCP server, framework adapters or HTTP. Warehouse Catalog readers Store MeasureFactLang OverlaysYAML Lineage Graph + scope Render Prompt Tools MCP Adapters HTTP Text equivalent of the diagram
  1. The warehouse is read by catalog readers, which write to the store.
  2. Measure (through FactLang), overlays (human YAML) and lineage also write to the store; measurement queries the warehouse.
  3. The join graph and question scoping read the store.
  4. Rendering turns the scoped result into a view.
  5. Agents receive it as a prompt, tools, an MCP server, framework adapters or HTTP.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page walks the shop warehouse from nothing to an agent-ready view. Every Python block on it runs as written (the docs test executes them), in a directory holding the shop warehouse as warehouse.duckdb and the example overlay as schemaguru.yaml; both are in the repository's examples/ folder (python examples/duckdb_quickstart.py builds the warehouse).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install 'schemaguru[duckdb]'

SchemaGuru needs Python 3.10+. Its only required dependencies are FactLang and PyYAML; every warehouse driver, LLM provider and agent framework is an optional extra (see the install matrix). FactLang (factlang>=0.1.4,<0.2) is installed from PyPI with it.

schemaguru doctor checks the installation. When the installed FactLang lacks a capability SchemaGuru uses (measurement, cost estimates, sampling, composite joins, metadata SQL), its factlang row is a WARN naming the missing ones; WARN rows do not fail the command (exit 0), only a FAIL does (exit 3).

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
print(guru)

Guru.connect opens the URL through FactLang's connect() when it is installed, and otherwise opens duckdb:// URLs with the DuckDB driver itself (read-only: SchemaGuru never writes to a warehouse, and a mistyped path does not create a file). Other warehouses open through FactLang's connect() (installed with SchemaGuru) and the warehouse's driver extra.

  • The store. Knowledge lives in one SQLite file, by default ./.schemaguru/<name>.db (name="default"). Pass store= to put it elsewhere.
  • First use crawls. When the store holds no table yet, connect crawls the catalog — metadata only (table and column names, types, keys, comments, catalog statistics). Where the warehouse bills metadata queries and the reader reports the bytes (BigQuery), they are admitted against Budget.crawl_bytes (default: no cap): at the cap the crawl stops with SG110 and the next crawl resumes. Readers that report no bytes are not counted. crawl=False skips it; crawl=True always crawls.
  • Paths. duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb is relative to the working directory; an absolute POSIX path takes four slashes, duckdb:////data/warehouse.duckdb.
  • DuckDB file names. DuckDB names a database's catalog after its file, so a file shop.duckdb holding a schema shop makes shop.orders ambiguous to DuckDB itself. Name the file differently from its schemas.

docs.title: Ask a question
docs.text:
view = guru.context("monthly revenue by customer segment")
print(view.text)
print(view.tokens, "tokens;", [t.canonical() for t in view.tables])

Before anything is measured, the view holds catalog knowledge and says so:

[shop.customers]
  unmeasured: nothing here has been measured yet; figures are declared or drafted
  1,000 rows (catalog stats)
  Columns:
    customer_id  INTEGER  PK (declared, enforced)
    email        VARCHAR
    phone        VARCHAR
    segment      VARCHAR
  Provenance: catalog only

[shop.orders]
  unmeasured: nothing here has been measured yet; figures are declared or drafted
  10,000 rows (catalog stats)
  Columns:
    order_id     INTEGER  PK (declared, enforced)
    customer_id  INTEGER
    account_id   INTEGER
    status       VARCHAR
    created_at   VARCHAR
    deleted      BOOLEAN
  Provenance: catalog only

Not shown: no other candidate tables.

context() never spends warehouse money by itself: tables it shows that were never measured are put on a queue (see Measure).

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
report = guru.measure("shop.orders")          # one table (names and globs accepted)
report = guru.measure(all=True)               # every table, hottest first
print(len(report.measured_tables), "tables measured;", report.bytes, "bytes")
for d in report.errors:
    print(d.code, d.message)

Measurement runs read-only FactLang probes within a budget (default: 1 GiB per probe, 10 GiB per run). Small tables are measured exactly; tables above 50 GiB (or 500M rows) are sampled and their numbers are labelled as estimates (Sampling).

Measurement needs FactLang's Checker.measure

SchemaGuru requires FactLang 0.1.4 or later, which provides it. With a FactLang build that lacks it, measure() writes nothing and returns SG304 in report.errors; everything else keeps working on catalog knowledge.

docs.title: Add what people know
docs.text:
A YAML overlay states what the data cannot: meaning, expected values, soft-delete rules, pitfalls, glossary terms. Expectations are checked against measurement and never rewritten.

for d in guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml"):
    print(d.code, d.severity.value, d.message, d.location)
print(guru.context("refund rate by month").text)

The [shop.orders] block of that view, after measurement and the overlay:

[shop.orders] One row per order placed on the storefront.
  ⚠ Pitfall: Refunds are a second row with negative amount. — fix: Filter amount > 0 for gross revenue.
  ⚠ WAIVED until 2027-01-31 (legacy upper-case rows being migrated): status: declared values 'paid','refunded','cancelled' — observed also 'PAID' (412 rows)
  ⚠ status: case drift: 'paid'/'PAID' differ only in case — compare case-insensitively
  ⚠ created_at: stored as VARCHAR, holds ISO-8601 date text (100% of values, measured 2026-11-24) — CAST before comparing
  Answers: revenue by month; average basket size
  10,000 rows (measured 2026-11-24)
  live rows: (deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted) (human, unchecked)
  Columns:
    order_id     INTEGER  PK (unique, measured 2026-11-24); ← shop.order_items.order_id (coverage 100%, measured 2026-11-24), ← shop.payments.order_id (coverage 5%, measured 2026-11-24); distinct 10,000 (measured 2026-11-24)
    customer_id  INTEGER  → shop.customers.customer_id N:1, match 98.04% (measured 2026-11-24); distinct 1,020 (measured 2026-11-24)
    account_id   INTEGER  → shop.accounts.account_id N:1, match 100%, coverage 40% (measured 2026-11-24); distinct 40 (measured 2026-11-24)
    status       VARCHAR  values: 'paid','refunded','cancelled' (+ observed 'PAID'); distinct 4 (measured 2026-11-24); Payment state of the order.
    created_at   VARCHAR  text holding ISO-8601 date text (see warning); note: ISO-8601 timestamp stored as STRING (human, unchecked); distinct 10,000 (measured 2026-11-24)
    deleted      BOOLEAN  values: TRUE (300) (measured 2026-11-24); null 97% (measured 2026-11-24); distinct 1 (measured 2026-11-24)
  Provenance: human overlay · measured 2026-11-24

docs.title: Bring your own connection
docs.text:
Guru.connect is a convenience. Any metadata executor and measurement backend can be passed in; here a DuckDB connection you already hold:

import duckdb

from schemaguru.catalog import DBAPIExecutor, reader_for

conn = duckdb.connect("warehouse.duckdb", read_only=True)
mine = sg.Guru(
    reader=reader_for("duckdb", DBAPIExecutor(conn)),
    store=".schemaguru/mine.db",
    dialect="duckdb",
)
print(mine.crawl().tables_seen, "tables crawled")
mine.close()
conn.close()

sg.Guru(connector=...) takes what your project already holds and builds both the catalog reader and the measurement backend from it: a DB-API connection (duckdb, sqlite3, psycopg, …; the dialect comes from the driver, or pass dialect=), a SQLAlchemy engine, a BigQuery client, a FactLang connector, or a plain function execute(sql) / execute(sql, params) returning rows as dicts (pass dialect=). A function that takes no parameters gets every value inlined as an ANSI literal. Such an execute(sql) or query(sql) host has no driver binding, so a probe whose text value holds a backslash, a NUL, a line terminator (CR, LF, U+0085, U+2028, U+2029), a quote look-alike a non-Unicode code page may read as ' (U+2018, U+2019, U+201A, U+201B, U+2032, U+02BC, U+FF07) or a backtick (some dialects read it as an identifier quote), or whose value is not a plain scalar, is refused (SG109), and its final SQL must pass the read-only guard. On BigQuery, Databricks, Spark, Hive and any dialect SchemaGuru does not know to double quotes, a text value holding ' is refused too: their string literals have no doubled-quote form (BigQuery rejects 'O''Brien', Databricks reads it as OBrien). Literals are spelled for the dialect (T-SQL text as N'…', T-SQL and Oracle booleans as 1/0), and each one is re-checked against that spelling before the host runs the SQL. Anything FactLang itself declines to inline is reported as SG109 with the reason. Pass a DB-API connection, an engine or a BigQuery client for full support. Anything else raises ConfigError SG107 naming the accepted types.

conn = duckdb.connect("warehouse.duckdb", read_only=True)
guru = sg.Guru(connector=conn, store=".schemaguru/mine.db")  # crawl, measure, context

docs.title: Extending SchemaGuru
docs.text:
Every component sits behind a small protocol (a structural type: implement the methods, no base class needed). Each page here gives the protocol, how to plug an implementation in, a worked example that runs, and a test template.

Extension point Protocol Plug in with Catalog reader — a new warehouse sg.catalog.CatalogReader sg.catalog.register_reader(dialect, factory) or Guru(reader=...) Store — where knowledge lives schemaguru.store.Store Guru(store=...) Retriever and embedder — how tables are found sg.scope.Retriever, sg.scope.Embedder Guru(retriever=...) Token counter sg.scope.TokenCounter Guru(token_counter=...) LLM provider — drafting sg.draft.LLMProvider guru.draft(..., provider=...) PII detector sg.pii.Detector sg.pii.register_detector(d) Failure classifier — runtime feedback schemaguru.feedback.FailureClassifier schemaguru.feedback.register_failure_classifier(c) or report_error(..., classifiers=[...]) Fact kind schemaguru.model.KindSpec schemaguru.model.register_fact_kind(spec) Render profile and format sg.render.Profile, a formatter sg.render.register_profile / register_format Change classifier — refresh schemaguru.refresh.ChangeClassifier schemaguru.refresh.register_change_classifier(c) Join candidate source sg.measure.JoinCandidateSource sg.measure.register_join_candidate_source(s) Server authenticator schemaguru.server.Authenticator create_app(guru, authenticator=...)

Discovery

Installed packages are discovered through entry-point groups schemaguru.<point> (readers, stores, retrievers, embedders, token_counters, llm_providers, pii_detectors, failure_classifiers, fact_kinds, profiles, formats, change_classifiers, join_candidate_sources, authenticators). Each registry loads its group lazily, once, on first use. A plugin that fails to import, or that its registry refuses (a duplicate name, a wrong shape), is skipped with diagnostic SG108 (guru.diagnostics, schemaguru.plugins.diagnostics()); it never raises. Points that are passed to a constructor (store, retriever, embedder, token counter, LLM provider, authenticator) are kept by name: schemaguru.plugins.get("retrievers", "mine") returns the factory, and schemaguru.plugins.register(point, name, factory) adds one in code.

[project.entry-points."schemaguru.readers"]
toyshop = "toyshop_sg:make_reader"

Rules every extension follows, because the rest of SchemaGuru relies on them:

  • Unknown is None. Never return 0, 1.0 or an empty string for something you do not know.
  • One bad item costs one item. Do not raise on bad data; report it (a Diagnostic, or leave the item out) and continue.
  • Timestamps are timezone-aware UTC. Naive datetimes are rejected.
  • Deterministic output. Equal inputs give equal outputs, in a stable order.

docs.title: Server authenticator
docs.text: Server mode asks an authenticator who is calling. The shipped one is BearerTokens; replace it to plug in your identity provider, an API gateway's headers, or mTLS information your proxy forwards.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class Authenticator(Protocol):
    def authenticate(self, headers: Mapping[str, str]) -> str | None:
        """The caller's role ("reader" or "admin"), or None when not authenticated."""

None answers 401 (SG805); "reader" on an admin route answers 403 (SG806). Never log or echo credentials, compare secrets in constant time, and fail closed: an exception or an unknown header shape means None.

docs.title: Worked example: trusting a gateway's verified header
docs.text:
A gateway in front of the server verifies the user and forwards X-Verified-Groups; the server trusts only requests that also carry the gateway's shared secret.

import hmac

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.server import create_app
from starlette.testclient import TestClient


class GatewayAuth:
    def __init__(self, secret: str) -> None:
        self._secret = secret.encode()

    def authenticate(self, headers):
        given = (headers.get("x-gateway-secret") or "").encode()
        if not hmac.compare_digest(given, self._secret):
            return None
        groups = {g.strip() for g in (headers.get("x-verified-groups") or "").split(",")}
        if "data-platform-admins" in groups:
            return "admin"
        return "reader" if "analysts" in groups else None


guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
app = create_app(guru, authenticator=GatewayAuth("s3cret-from-the-vault"))
with TestClient(app) as client:
    ok = {"x-gateway-secret": "s3cret-from-the-vault", "x-verified-groups": "analysts"}
    print(client.get("/search", params={"q": "orders"}, headers=ok).json()["text"])
    print(client.get("/search", params={"q": "orders"}).status_code)
    print(client.post("/refresh", json={}, headers=ok).status_code)
guru.close()

    assert auth.authenticate({"x-gateway-secret": "s3cret", "x-verified-groups": "analysts"}) == "reader"

docs.title: Catalog reader
docs.text: A reader teaches SchemaGuru a new warehouse's catalog. It is metadata-only: it reads system views (or a client API), never data rows, and answers None for what it does not know.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class CatalogReader(Protocol):
    dialect: str
    def list_catalogs(self) -> Iterator[str]: ...            # may yield nothing
    def list_schemas(self, catalog: str | None, *, page_token: str | None) -> Page[Schema]: ...
    def list_tables(self, schema: Schema, *, page_token: str | None,
                    changed_since: datetime | None) -> Page[Table]: ...
    def columns(self, tables: Sequence[ObjectRef]) -> Mapping[ObjectRef, list[Column]]: ...
    def constraints(self, tables: Sequence[ObjectRef]) -> Mapping[ObjectRef, list[Constraint]]: ...
    def capabilities(self) -> ReaderCapabilities: ...
  • list_tables returns every live table when changed_since is None; otherwise only those altered since (meaningful only when capabilities().incremental is true).
  • columns and constraints are batched: the crawl passes up to column_batch tables.
  • Optional view_definitions(tables) -> Mapping[ObjectRef, str] (set ReaderCapabilities(view_definitions=True)): the SQL text of views and materialized views, batched like columns. Leave both out and the reader works unchanged. A definition you cannot read is absent, never guessed; the text is raw SQL that may hold PII, so never log it or put it in an error.
  • Page(items, next_token): next_token=None on the last page. List in a stable order, so an interrupted crawl can resume.
  • Raise CatalogError(code, message) for a failure of the whole call; the crawl records it (SG102) and skips that schema, page or batch.
  • Column.family is a FactLang type family (integer, decimal, float, string, boolean, date, timestamp, …).

docs.title: Worked example: a catalog from a dict
docs.text:
A reader for a system that publishes its catalog as JSON (here, an in-memory dict).

from collections.abc import Iterator, Mapping, Sequence
from datetime import datetime

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.catalog import Page, ReaderCapabilities, register_reader
from schemaguru.model.structure import Column, Constraint, Schema, Table

CATALOG = {
    "shop": {
        "orders": [("order_id", "BIGINT", "integer"), ("status", "TEXT", "string")],
        "customers": [("customer_id", "BIGINT", "integer"), ("segment", "TEXT", "string")],
    }
}


class DictReader:
    dialect = "dictdb"

    def __init__(self, catalog: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, list]]) -> None:
        self.catalog = catalog

    def list_catalogs(self) -> Iterator[str]:
        return iter(())

    def list_schemas(self, catalog: str | None, *, page_token: str | None) -> Page[Schema]:
        return Page([Schema(None, name) for name in sorted(self.catalog)])

    def list_tables(self, schema: Schema, *, page_token: str | None,
                    changed_since: datetime | None) -> Page[Table]:
        names = sorted(self.catalog.get(schema.name, {}))
        return Page([Table(sg.ObjectRef(None, schema.name, n), "table") for n in names])

    def columns(self, tables: Sequence[sg.ObjectRef]) -> Mapping[sg.ObjectRef, list[Column]]:
        out = {}
        for t in tables:
            cols = self.catalog[t.schema][t.table]
            out[t] = [Column(sg.ObjectRef(None, t.schema, t.table, name), i, native, family)
                      for i, (name, native, family) in enumerate(cols, start=1)]
        return out

    def constraints(self, tables: Sequence[sg.ObjectRef]) -> Mapping[sg.ObjectRef, list[Constraint]]:
        return {t: [Constraint("primary_key", t, (self.catalog[t.schema][t.table][0][0],))]
                for t in tables}

    def capabilities(self) -> ReaderCapabilities:
        return ReaderCapabilities(constraints=True)


guru = sg.Guru(reader=DictReader(CATALOG), store=".schemaguru/dict.db", dialect="dictdb")
print(guru.crawl().tables_seen, [t.ref.canonical() for t in guru.store.iter_tables()])
print(guru.context("orders by status").text)
guru.close()

To have Guru(connector=...) and reader_for(dialect, executor) build it, register a factory taking a metadata executor (execute(sql, params) → rows; see sg.catalog.MetadataExecutor):

register_reader("dictdb", lambda executor: DictReader(CATALOG))
print("dictdb" in sg.catalog.dialects())

A SQL-backed reader runs its metadata queries through the executor it is given — a FactLangExecutor over a FactLang connector, or a DBAPIExecutor over a DB-API connection — always with bind parameters for values. The shipped readers in schemaguru/catalog/readers/ are the reference.

def test_reader_contract():
    reader = DictReader(CATALOG)
    schemas = reader.list_schemas(None, page_token=None)
    assert schemas.next_token is None and [s.name for s in schemas.items] == ["shop"]
    tables = reader.list_tables(schemas.items[0], page_token=None, changed_since=None).items
    cols = reader.columns([t.ref for t in tables])
    assert all(c.ref.table == t.ref.table for t in tables for c in cols[t.ref])
    # unknown stays None, never a default
    assert all(t.row_count is None for t in tables)

docs.title: Change classifier
docs.text: Refresh classifies every change between two snapshots as BENIGN, REVIEW, PRE_EXISTING or NOT_MEASURED. A change classifier adds your own rules.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class ChangeClassifier(Protocol):
    def classify(self, change: Change, prev_effective: Eff, new_effective: Eff) -> ChangeClass | None:
        """None means no opinion; the next classifier (finally the default) decides."""

A Change has kind (a KindSpec), subject, before and after (facts or None) and change ("added", "removed", "value" or "status"). prev_effective / new_effective are the resolved knowledge of both snapshots, keyed (kind name, subject key).

Order of judgement: NOT_MEASURED first (a check that did not run is never "removed" or "fixed" — no classifier can override that), then registered classifiers in registration order (the first with an opinion wins), then the default rules. Register with schemaguru.refresh.register_change_classifier(c); reset_change_classifiers() removes all.

docs.title: Worked example: row counts of reloaded tables are not news
docs.text:
from schemaguru.refresh import ChangeClass, classify_change, register_change_classifier


class RowCountsMove:
    """Tables in `shop` are reloaded nightly: a row count that changes or disappears
    between snapshots is expected, not a finding."""

    def classify(self, change, prev_effective, new_effective):
        if change.kind.name == "ROW_COUNT" and change.subject.schema == "shop":
            return ChangeClass.BENIGN
        return None


register_change_classifier(RowCountsMove())

# what refresh does for one change: a row count that disappeared (by default: REVIEW)
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from schemaguru.knowledge import Change
from schemaguru.model import Fact, FactKind, ObjectRef, Provenance, Status

at = datetime(2026, 11, 24, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
ref = ObjectRef(None, "shop", "orders")
before = Fact.make(FactKind.ROW_COUNT, ref, {"rows": 100}, Provenance.MEASURED,
                   Status.OBSERVED, method="exact", observed_at=at)
change = Change(FactKind.ROW_COUNT, ref, before, None, "removed")
print(classify_change(change, {}, {}))          # BENIGN: our rule had an opinion

classify_change(change, prev_effective, new_effective) runs the whole chain for one change, which is what a unit test calls.

docs.title: Fact kind
docs.text: Fact kinds are an open registry. Add one for knowledge the built-ins do not cover — an owner, a data-retention class, a cost centre — and store it like any other fact.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class KindSpec:
    name: str
    subject: Literal["table", "column", "join", "global"]
    meaning: bool          # HUMAN beats DRAFTED (precedence rule 1)
    expectation: bool      # never replaced by measurement; checked (rule 2)
    identity_fields: tuple[str, ...] | None = None   # payload keys that define the fact id

identity_fields=None makes the whole value part of the fact's id; a tuple names only those keys, so a re-measured number updates the same fact instead of creating another. Register with schemaguru.model.register_fact_kind(spec) (a duplicate name raises unless replace=True); get_kind(name) looks one up.

docs.title: Built-in kinds
docs.text:
Kind Subject Identity fields DESCRIPTION, USE_CASES, ENTITY_TYPE, PITFALL table whole value (meaning) GLOSSARY global whole value (meaning) PRIMARY_KEY table columns (expectation) JOIN join none (expectation) VALUES column case_sensitive, split (expectation) SOFT_DELETE table predicate (expectation) NULL_RATE, DISTINCT column none ROW_COUNT table none FRESHNESS table column TYPE_NOTE column stored_as, means PII column category METRIC, WAYPOINT_RULE global whole value NEVER_QUERY table whole value LINEAGE table upstream, ignore COLUMN_LINEAGE column inputs, ignore

LINEAGE and COLUMN_LINEAGE are declared (dbt), parsed (view definitions) or written by a human (overlay), and their status is always UNVERIFIED: a lineage fact that is MEASURED or DRAFTED, or whose status is anything else, raises. The fact's source is not part of its id. schemaguru.model.resolve_lineage applies their precedence per subject and level: a human list replaces the parsed ones, a human ignore hides them (all of them, or only an exactly equal list), and equal parsed lists from dbt and a view merge into one link naming both sources.

docs.title: Worked example: data owners
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.model import Fact, KindSpec, Provenance, Status, register_fact_kind

OWNER = KindSpec("OWNER", "table", meaning=True, expectation=False, identity_fields=())
register_fact_kind(OWNER)

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
orders = guru.table_ref("orders")
guru.store.put_facts([Fact.make(OWNER, orders, {"team": "checkout"}, Provenance.HUMAN,
                                Status.UNVERIFIED, source="owners.csv:2",
                                observed_at=datetime(2026, 11, 24, tzinfo=timezone.utc))])
for f in guru.store.facts_for([orders], ["OWNER"]):
    print(f.kind.name, f.value["team"], f.provenance.value, f.source)
guru.close()

Custom kinds take part in resolution, snapshots, diffs and refresh reports like the built-ins. To show one in views, render it in a profile.

docs.title: Failure classifier
docs.text: A failure classifier reads one failed query and its error message and says which table and column the failure is about, so runtime feedback can prioritise them.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FeedbackRecord:
    table: ObjectRef | None
    column: str | None
    failure_class: Literal["type_mismatch", "unknown_column", "unknown_table", "ambiguous_column"]

class FailureClassifier(Protocol):
    def classify(self, sql: str, error: str, dialect: str | None) -> list[FeedbackRecord]: ...

Return an empty list when the message is not yours. A classifier that raises contributes nothing (the intake never raises). Records hold identifiers only; the SQL is never stored. The built-ins are schemaguru.feedback.BUILTIN_CLASSIFIERS.

docs.title: Worked example: DuckDB comparison errors
docs.text:
DuckDB's "Cannot compare values of type VARCHAR and type DATE" carries no position, so the built-in type_mismatch classifier records nothing for it. A dialect-specific classifier can use a narrower rule — here, the one column compared with a DATE literal:

import re

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.feedback import BUILTIN_CLASSIFIERS, FeedbackRecord, report_error


class DuckDBCompare:
    _err = re.compile(r"Cannot compare values of type (\w+) and type (\w+)")
    _cmp = re.compile(r"(\w+)\.(\w+)\s*[<>=]+\s*DATE\s*'", re.I)
    _from = re.compile(r"FROM\s+(\w+)\.(\w+)\s+(?:AS\s+)?(\w+)", re.I)

    def classify(self, sql, error, dialect):
        if dialect != "duckdb" or not self._err.search(error):
            return []
        cmp, frm = self._cmp.search(sql), self._from.search(sql)
        if not (cmp and frm and cmp.group(1) == frm.group(3)):
            return []
        table = sg.ObjectRef(None, frm.group(1), frm.group(2))
        return [FeedbackRecord(table, cmp.group(2), "type_mismatch")]


guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
sql = "SELECT count(*) FROM shop.orders o WHERE o.created_at > DATE '2025-06-01'"
err = "Binder Error: Cannot compare values of type VARCHAR and type DATE"
n = report_error(guru.store, sql, err, "duckdb",
                 classifiers=[*BUILTIN_CLASSIFIERS, DuckDBCompare()])
print(n, guru.feedback_summary())
guru.close()

Pass the built-ins along with yours: classifiers= replaces the default list. Guru.report_error uses the built-ins only; call schemaguru.feedback.report_error (as above) to use your own.

docs.text:
def test_classifier():
    c = DuckDBCompare()
    sql = "SELECT 1 FROM shop.orders o WHERE o.created_at > DATE '2025-01-01'"
    err = "Cannot compare values of type VARCHAR and type DATE"
    [rec] = c.classify(sql, err, "duckdb")
    assert (rec.table.table, rec.column, rec.failure_class) == ("orders", "created_at", "type_mismatch")
    assert c.classify(sql, "some other error", "duckdb") == []
    assert c.classify(sql, err, "postgres") == []

docs.title: Join candidate source
docs.text:
A join is measured only if something proposes it. Candidates come from these sources, in priority order (schemaguru.measure.join_candidates):

  1. declared foreign keys from the catalog;
  2. joins in overlays (tables.<t>.joins) and dbt relationships tests (DECLARED);
  3. registered JoinCandidateSource plug-ins;
  4. name and type heuristics: x_id / xId / x_fk → a table x or xs with a compatible key, and a column named like another table's single-column primary key in the same schema (at most 5 per column, same catalog only);
  5. join candidates in LLM drafts.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
sg.measure.JoinCandidateSource: a name: str and candidates(store, table), returning JoinRefs with table on the left (child) side. It only reads. Register one with sg.measure.register_join_candidate_source(source), or install it through the entry-point group schemaguru.join_candidate_sources. A proposal is measured before anything is shown; one that fails measurement leaves only a diagnostic, like a heuristic guess. A source that raises costs only its proposals.

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.model import JoinRef, ObjectRef


class Lineage:
    name = "lineage"

    def candidates(self, store, table):
        if table.table == "ref_child":
            yield JoinRef((ObjectRef(None, "shop", "ref_child", "parent_id"),),
                          (ObjectRef(None, "shop", "ref_parent", "id"),))


sg.measure.register_join_candidate_source(Lineage())

Joins you also want shown as human expectations (a broken one is then a contradiction, not a silent drop) belong in an overlay instead, as below.

docs.title: Worked example: a join the heuristics cannot see
docs.text:
In the shop, ref_child.parent_id points at ref_parent.id. No table is called parent, so the name heuristics miss it, and the warehouse declares no foreign key. Propose it from a generated overlay:

from pathlib import Path

import schemaguru as sg

Path("generated-joins.yaml").write_text(
    "version: 1\n"
    "tables:\n"
    "  shop.ref_child:\n"
    "    joins:\n"
    "      - from: parent_id\n"
    "        to: shop.ref_parent.id\n"
    "        cardinality: N:1\n",
    encoding="utf-8",
)

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
print(guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml", "generated-joins.yaml"))
guru.measure("shop.ref_child")
for f in guru.store.facts_for(None, ["JOIN"]):
    if f.subject.left[0].table == "ref_child" and f.subject.left[0].column == "parent_id":
        print(f.provenance.value, f.status.value, f.value.get("match_rate"),
              f.value.get("coverage"))
guru.close()

The human join stays as written (an expectation, never rewritten); measurement adds a MEASURED join fact beside it — forward match 100%, reverse coverage 0.3% in the shop, a correct but very asymmetric join — and only the measured fact makes it a path-search edge.

    overlay.write_text(render_overlay(my_join_source()), encoding="utf-8")

docs.title: LLM provider
docs.text: Drafting calls an LLM through one small protocol, so any model, gateway or local server fits.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class LLMProvider(Protocol):
    name: str
    def complete_json(self, system: str, user: str, schema: dict, *, max_tokens: int) -> dict: ...
    async def acomplete_json(self, system: str, user: str, schema: dict, *, max_tokens: int) -> dict: ...
  • Return a dict matching schema (the drafting JSON schema, schemaguru.draft.DRAFT_SCHEMA). Raise schemaguru.draft.InvalidReply for a reply that is not such an object: the pipeline retries once, then records an ERROR draft for those tables (SG401). Any other exception is a provider failure (SG403).
  • Optionally expose model: str (recorded on drafted facts) and last_usage: Usage (input/output tokens of the last call); without usage, tokens are estimated from length.
  • user is a JSON document already masked by the value policy; send it as given.

Shipped: AnthropicProvider, OpenAICompatibleProvider, and CallableProvider(fn) for wrapping a function (sync or async; it may return a dict, JSON text, or (reply, Usage)).

docs.title: Worked example: a provider class
docs.text:
A provider for an in-house gateway; the network call is replaced by a stub so this runs offline.

import json

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.draft import InvalidReply, Usage


class GatewayProvider:
    name = "gateway"
    model = "house-model-1"

    def __init__(self, post):
        self.post, self.last_usage = post, None

    def complete_json(self, system, user, schema, *, max_tokens):
        reply = self.post({"system": system, "user": user, "schema": schema,
                           "max_tokens": max_tokens})
        try:
            data = json.loads(reply["text"])
        except ValueError as e:
            raise InvalidReply(f"not JSON: {e}") from None
        self.last_usage = Usage(reply["in"], reply["out"])
        return data

    async def acomplete_json(self, system, user, schema, *, max_tokens):
        return self.complete_json(system, user, schema, max_tokens=max_tokens)


def fake_gateway(request):
    tables = json.loads(request["user"])["tables"]
    drafts = [{"table": t["table"], "description": "One row per item in a basket.",
               "columns": [], "use_cases": [], "entity_type": None, "pitfalls": [],
               "soft_delete": None, "type_notes": [], "pii": [], "join_candidates": [],
               "glossary": []} for t in tables]
    return {"text": json.dumps({"tables": drafts}), "in": 900, "out": 120}


provider = GatewayProvider(fake_gateway)
guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
report = guru.draft("shop.order_items", provider=provider)
print(report.calls, report.input_tokens, report.output_tokens, report.errors)
print(guru.handle_tool_call("describe_table", {"table": "order_items"})["text"].splitlines()[0])
guru.close()

docs.title: Test template
docs.text:
Check your provider against the schema it is given, on a scripted transport:

from schemaguru.draft import DRAFT_SCHEMA, validate

def test_provider_returns_schema_valid_json():
    p = GatewayProvider(fake_gateway)
    user = json.dumps({"tables": [{"table": "shop.orders"}]})
    out = p.complete_json("system", user, DRAFT_SCHEMA, max_tokens=1000)
    assert validate(out, DRAFT_SCHEMA) == []      # the list of violations
    assert p.last_usage is not None

docs.title: PII detector
docs.text: Detectors decide which values are personal and get masked to a shape. Add one for an identifier format your organisation uses.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class Detector(Protocol):
    name: str          # unique; shown as the PII fact's detector
    category: str      # email, phone, name, address, gov_id, card, iban, ip, free_text, other
    def matches(self, value: str) -> bool: ...

matches sees one whole value (strip it yourself if whitespace matters) and must be fast and safe on hostile input — the built-ins are tested against 50,000-character adversarial strings. Register with sg.pii.register_detector(d) (a duplicate name raises unless replace=True); sg.pii.reset_detectors() restores the built-in set. Plug-ins run after the built-ins.

docs.title: Worked example: customer numbers
docs.text:
import re

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.pii import classify_column, mask_value, register_detector


class CustomerNumber:
    name = "customer_number"
    category = "gov_id"
    _rx = re.compile(r"CUS-\d{6}-[A-Z]")

    def matches(self, value: str) -> bool:
        return self._rx.fullmatch(value.strip()) is not None


register_detector(CustomerNumber())
print(mask_value("CUS-104233-K"))
print(classify_column([("CUS-104233-K", 3), ("CUS-551100-B", 2)], distinct=2, name="ref"))

When a measured column's observed values match, the column gets a PII fact (MEASURED, detector=customer_number), its values are masked everywhere they leave SchemaGuru, and the agent is told the column holds personal data. Detection is by value shape; a column name alone never classifies a column.

docs.title: Render profile and format
docs.text: A profile decides how one table is written for one kind of reader; a format decides how a whole view is serialised. Both are registries.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
class Profile(Protocol):
    def render_table(self, eff: TableKnowledge, level: DetailLevel) -> str: ...

Formatter = Callable[[ContextView], str]

TableKnowledge carries one table's structure (ref, table, columns, constraints) and its effective knowledge (eff.get(kind, column=None) returns the resolved Effective for a kind), plus now and config. level is the detail level the budget fit asks for (FULL, STANDARD, LITE, NAME_ONLY); the fit tries richer levels first and keeps the first that fits, so a lower level must never be longer than a higher one.

Register with sg.render.register_profile(name, profile) and sg.render.register_format(name, fn); use them as guru.context(q, profile=name) and guru.context(q, format=name) / str(view).

Keep the outbound sweep

The built-in profiles end with schemaguru.render.profiles.finish(eff, text), which runs the value policy's shape sweep. A custom profile that shows values must do the same.

docs.title: Worked example: a one-line-per-table profile and a YAML format
docs.text:
import yaml

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.model.detail import DetailLevel
from schemaguru.render import register_format, register_profile
from schemaguru.render.profiles import finish


class OneLine:
    def render_table(self, eff, level):
        if level is DetailLevel.NAME_ONLY:
            return eff.ref.canonical()
        rows = eff.get("ROW_COUNT")
        n = rows.primary.value.get("rows") if rows is not None and rows.primary else None
        cols = ", ".join(c.ref.column for c in eff.columns)
        return finish(eff, f"{eff.ref.canonical()} ({'?' if n is None else n} rows): {cols}")


def to_yaml(view):
    return yaml.safe_dump({"question": view.question, "fingerprint": view.fingerprint,
                           "blocks": [b.text for b in view.blocks]}, sort_keys=True)


register_profile("oneline", OneLine())
register_format("yaml", to_yaml)

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure("shop.payments")
print(guru.context("payments per order", profile="oneline").text)
print(str(guru.context("payments per order", format="yaml"))[:160])
guru.close()

docs.title: Retriever and embedder
docs.text: The retriever picks the seed tables for a question (step 1 of scoping).

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class Retriever(Protocol):
    def search(self, question: str, k: int) -> list[tuple[ObjectRef, float]]: ...

class Embedder(Protocol):
    @property
    def model_id(self) -> str: ...                 # names the model and version
    def embed(self, texts: Sequence[str]) -> list[list[float]]: ...

Return at most k (table ref, score) pairs, highest score first, ties in a stable order; only tables that exist in the store. Shipped: LexicalRetriever(store) (the default), EmbeddingRetriever(store, embedder) (extra embeddings, numpy), and HybridRetriever(*retrievers, k_rrf=60) (reciprocal-rank fusion).

docs.title: Worked example: a synonym retriever, fused with the default
docs.text:
import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.scope import HybridRetriever, LexicalRetriever


class SynonymRetriever:
    """Maps business words to tables the names do not reveal."""

    def __init__(self, store, synonyms: dict[str, list[str]]) -> None:
        self.store, self.synonyms = store, synonyms

    def search(self, question: str, k: int) -> list[tuple[sg.ObjectRef, float]]:
        hits: dict[sg.ObjectRef, float] = {}
        for word in question.lower().split():
            for name in self.synonyms.get(word.strip("?,."), []):
                ref = sg.ObjectRef.parse(name)
                if self.store.table(ref) is not None:
                    hits[ref] = hits.get(ref, 0.0) + 1.0
        ranked = sorted(hits.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0].canonical()))
        return ranked[:k]


guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
synonyms = {"clicks": ["shop.events"], "baskets": ["shop.order_items"]}
guru.retriever = HybridRetriever(LexicalRetriever(guru.store),
                                 SynonymRetriever(guru.store, synonyms))
print([t.table for t in guru.context("clicks and baskets per day").tables])

Pass it at construction with sg.Guru(..., retriever=...); assigning guru.retriever as above works too, as long as no view for the same question was cached yet.

docs.title: Worked example: an embedder
docs.text:
EmbeddingRetriever stores one vector per table document in the store, keyed by model_id, and re-embeds only tables whose document changed. Any model fits behind Embedder; this toy one hashes words into a small vector so the example runs offline:

import hashlib

from schemaguru.scope import EmbeddingRetriever


class HashingEmbedder:
    model_id = "hashing-64-v1"

    def embed(self, texts):
        out = []
        for text in texts:
            v = [0.0] * 64
            for word in text.lower().split():
                v[int(hashlib.sha256(word.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 64] += 1.0
            out.append(v)
        return out


emb = EmbeddingRetriever(guru.store, HashingEmbedder())
print(emb.index(), "tables embedded")
print([(r.table, round(s, 3)) for r, s in emb.search("payments for an order", 3)])
guru.close()

docs.title: Store
docs.text:
The store holds everything SchemaGuru knows: structure, facts, snapshots, the crawl checkpoint, the budget ledger and the feedback queue. Two backends ship:

  • SQLiteStore(path) — the default; one file, WAL mode, FTS5 search (a LIKE fallback with SG701 where FTS5 is missing).
  • PostgresStore(dsn, schema=None) (extra postgres-store) — the same schema, weighted tsvector search; for teams and server mode.

Migrations are numbered SQL files applied on open; a store written by a newer schema version than the library knows is refused (SG702).

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: schemaguru.store.Store (about 30 methods) covers CRUD over the model plus search(query, k), facts_for(subjects, kinds), put_facts, delete_facts, snapshots and diffs, crawl_state, the budget ledger, the feedback queue and transactions. Every write is an idempotent upsert keyed on stable ids; every listing is in a stable order. Read the protocol's docstrings in schemaguru/store/protocol.py before implementing it.

docs.title: The lineage index (optional)
docs.text:
schemaguru.store.LineageIndex is a second, runtime-checkable protocol that both shipped stores implement; lineage_index(store) returns the store as one, or None. It answers lineage questions in the store, never by scanning facts in Python:

  • lineage_edges(keys, direction=..., level=...) — "upstream" returns the edges whose downstream_key is in keys, "downstream" those whose upstream_key is; level is "table" or "column". Sorted by (downstream_key, upstream_key, fact_id).
  • lineage_state_get(refs) / lineage_state_set({ref: sha256 or None}) — the view-definition hash each table's lineage was last parsed from (None deletes the row).

The index holds effective lineage only (schemaguru.model.lineage.resolve_lineage: a human replacement or ignore wins over dbt and parsed views). Inside the same transaction as put_facts / delete_facts, the store recomputes every touched subject's edges from all of its LINEAGE / COLUMN_LINEAGE facts, so a rolled-back write leaves no edges behind. The shipped stores keep it in the lineage_edges table (SQLite migration 3, Postgres migration 2; a store written by 0.1.0 migrates on open and keeps its facts unchanged).

A custom store need not implement it: everything else works, but downstream lineage is unavailable (SG705). A wrapper that delegates to a shipped store can expose it by delegating these three methods too.

docs.title: Plugging one in
docs.text:
Any object implementing the protocol can be passed as Guru(store=...); a str or path opens a SQLiteStore. A thin wrapper is the easiest worked example — here one that counts fact writes (for metrics) and delegates the rest:

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.store import SQLiteStore


class CountingStore:
    def __init__(self, inner):
        self.inner, self.fact_writes = inner, 0

    def put_facts(self, facts):
        facts = list(facts)
        self.fact_writes += len(facts)
        return self.inner.put_facts(facts)

    def __getattr__(self, name):          # everything else: delegate
        return getattr(self.inner, name)


store = CountingStore(SQLiteStore(".schemaguru/counted.db"))
guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", store=store)
guru.measure("shop.orders")
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")
print(store.fact_writes, "facts written")
guru.close()
store.inner.close()

A Guru closes only a store it opened itself; close yours when you are done.

docs.title: Token counter
docs.text: Views are fitted to a token budget; the counter decides what a token is.

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text:
class TokenCounter(Protocol):
    def count(self, text: str) -> int: ...

Shipped: CharTokenCounter (default, ceil(len(text) / 4)) and TiktokenCounter (extra tiktoken; select it with Config(token_counter="tiktoken")). The count must be deterministic and monotone enough that a longer text never counts fewer tokens than its prefix — the budget fit relies on it.

docs.title: Worked example: a conservative word counter
docs.text:
import math

import schemaguru as sg


class WordCounter:
    """Over-estimates: 1.4 tokens per whitespace-separated word, plus one per line."""

    def count(self, text: str) -> int:
        return math.ceil(1.4 * len(text.split())) + text.count("\n")


import duckdb

from schemaguru.catalog import DBAPIExecutor, reader_for

conn = duckdb.connect("warehouse.duckdb", read_only=True)
guru = sg.Guru(reader=reader_for("duckdb", DBAPIExecutor(conn)), dialect="duckdb",
               token_counter=WordCounter())
guru.crawl()
view = guru.context("orders by status", budget_tokens=300)
print(view.tokens, "tokens by WordCounter;", [t.table for t in view.tables])
guru.close()
conn.close()

Guru(token_counter=...) takes precedence over Config.token_counter.

docs.title: Agents, tools and MCP
docs.text: SchemaGuru gives an agent knowledge three ways: a view in the prompt, tools it can call, and an MCP server any MCP client can use. All three show the same knowledge through the same value policy.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
guru.tools() returns JSON-schema tool specs (name, description, input_schema); guru.handle_tool_call(name, args) runs one and always returns a JSON-safe dict with a text field for the model — errors included, it never raises.

Tool Returns schema_context the question-scoped view (Scoping); call it first search_tables ranked tables with one-line descriptions describe_table everything known about one table find_join_path measured routes with join keys (and a SQL snippet when FactLang renders one), or the refusal column_values observed and declared values of a column, as the value policy allows check_fact runs a FactLang claim on the warehouse, under the measurement budget explain_term a glossary term or metric and the tables it maps to lineage what a table or column is built from (upstream) or feeds (downstream), from dbt manifests, view definitions and overlays; declared or parsed, never measured, never a join path. nodes, edges (each with source and transform), cycles, and truncated at 200 nodes

The lineage tool takes ref, direction (upstream or downstream), depth (1 to 5) and level; see Lineage.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure(all=True)
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")

print([t["name"] for t in guru.tools()])
for name, args in [
    ("search_tables", {"query": "refunds"}),
    ("column_values", {"column": "orders.status"}),
    ("explain_term", {"term": "active customer"}),
    ("find_join_path", {"from": "orders", "to": "events"}),
    ("describe_table", {"table": "nope"}),
]:
    result = guru.handle_tool_call(name, args)
    print(f"--- {name}:", result.get("error", "ok"))
    print(result["text"])
  • check_fact spends, so it is off by default. It is the one tool that runs on the warehouse. Config(agent_checks="allow") turns it on; every call is then priced and admitted through the Guru's one per-period budget (shared with the background drainer, refilled per Budget.period_s) and recorded in the ledger. It also needs a FactLang that publishes its factlang_check tool definition. Its evidence reaches the agent as an allow-list only: verdict, claim text and SQL template with literals as ?, bytes, duration.
  • Names are resolved, never guessed. A bare name matching several tables returns an error listing the candidates.
  • Errors are results: SG803 for an unknown tool or invalid arguments, SG804 for an unexpected failure (its type and a masked message).
  • Every result passes the renderer's value policy, the outbound shape sweep and free-text masking (PII).

docs.title: The prompt block
docs.text:
guru.prompt_block() is a system-prompt fragment: the tools, how to use them, the global blocks and the legend. With a question it appends that question's view.

You can inspect the data warehouse with these tools:
- schema_context: The warehouse tables, columns, measured joins and hazards relevant to a question. Call this first, before writing SQL.
- search_tables: Ranked tables matching a text query, each with a one-line description.
- describe_table: Everything known about one table: columns, keys, joins, values, pitfalls.
- find_join_path: Measured join routes between two tables with join keys and a SQL snippet, or the reason there is none. Never invent a join this tool does not return.
- column_values: Observed and declared values of one column, as the value policy allows them.
- explain_term: What a business term or metric means and which tables it maps to.
- lineage: Which tables and columns a table or column is built from (upstream) or feeds (downstream), from dbt manifests, view definitions and overlays. Declared or parsed, never measured; not a join path.
How to use them:
- Call schema_context with the user's question before writing SQL; use only the tables, columns and joins it shows, and heed every ⚠ line.
- Use search_tables when a table you need is not in the view, then describe_table for its full block.
- Join only along routes find_join_path returns; a refusal means there is no safe route. Never guess a join key or a table name: a bare name that matches several tables comes back as an error listing the candidates.
- Use column_values before filtering on a coded column; values may be masked by policy.
- Use explain_term for business terms and metrics.
- Use `lineage` to see what a table or column is built from or feeds; it is declared or parsed, never measured, and never a join path.

Legend:
  ⚠ a hazard: measured, declared by a person, or drafted (then marked (draft)).
  ≈ / ≥ estimated from a sample of a large table; never verified.
  (draft) written by a language model and not checked.
  measured <date> an observed number; verified <date> a claim that passed its check.
  (human, unchecked) / (declared, unchecked) stated by a person or a declaration; not yet checked against the data.
  Absence of a warning is not verification.

docs.text:
Each adapter only maps guru.tools() onto a framework's tool type (one extra each, imported lazily); the dispatch is always handle_tool_call.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
schemaguru mcp (extra mcp, MCP SDK ≥ 2.3) serves the tools plus a resource per table, schema://tables/{ref} (the describe_table text), over stdio:

schemaguru --store .schemaguru/shop.db mcp                     # from the store only
schemaguru --url duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb --store .schemaguru/shop.db mcp   # warehouse attached

Client configuration and an in-process check: examples/mcp_server.md. From Python, schemaguru.agent.mcp.serve(guru) serves a Guru you configured (with its overlays loaded).

guru.close()

docs.title: Guarding the agent's SQL
docs.text: SchemaGuru does not run agent SQL. If your host does, run it under a read-only warehouse role; sg.guard.check_sql is a best-effort pre-check on top, not a sandbox — see Security.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: SchemaGuru keeps everything it knows about a warehouse as facts in a local store, and renders the slice a question needs as a view. Five ideas explain almost every behaviour.

docs.title: Facts
docs.text:
A Fact is one statement about one subject — a table, a column, a join, or the warehouse as a whole (glossary terms, metrics):

Field Meaning kind what is stated: ROW_COUNT, NULL_RATE, DISTINCT, VALUES, JOIN, PRIMARY_KEY, FRESHNESS, TYPE_NOTE, SOFT_DELETE, PII, DESCRIPTION, USE_CASES, ENTITY_TYPE, PITFALL, GLOSSARY, METRIC, NEVER_QUERY, WAYPOINT_RULE, LINEAGE, COLUMN_LINEAGE (an open registry: add your own) value the kind's payload; a field that is not known is None, never a default provenance where it came from (below) status how far it is established (below) method how a measured number was measured: exact, or sampled:<method>:<fraction>:<seed> evidence the FactLang outcome: claim text, verdict, numbers; SQL kept as a template only source, observed_at e.g. overlay:schemaguru.yaml:12; a timezone-aware UTC time

The id of a fact is a content hash, so re-measuring a number updates the same fact instead of piling up copies.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure("shop.orders")                    # MEASURED facts
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")          # HUMAN facts
orders = guru.table_ref("orders")              # bare names resolve when unambiguous
for f in guru.store.facts_for([orders], ["ROW_COUNT", "SOFT_DELETE"]):
    print(f.kind.name, f.provenance.value, f.status.value, f.method, dict(f.value))

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Provenance Meaning Typical facts CATALOG read from the warehouse's system catalog columns, types, declared keys, statistics DECLARED declared by metadata outside the warehouse dbt descriptions and tests MEASURED computed by a FactLang probe on the data match rates, null rates, observed values DRAFTED written by an LLM; always marked (draft) until checked or accepted descriptions, pitfalls, soft-delete guesses HUMAN written by a person in an overlay, or an accepted draft meaning, expected values, rules

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Status Meaning Rendered as OBSERVED a measured number (no predicate to pass) measured <date> VERIFIED a FactLang claim passed verified <date> CONTRADICTED a claim failed: the data disagrees a ⚠ warning UNVERIFIED drafted or declared, not checked (yet, or not checkable) (draft), (human, unchecked) ESTIMATED measured on a sample of a large table ≈ 3.2% (sampled 1%, ±0.4%) — never verified UNMEASURABLE nothing to measure, e.g. an empty table unmeasurable: … ERROR the probe failed, or was over budget the reason STALE observed or verified, but older than the TTL (14 days) still shown, flagged WAIVED a contradiction a person acknowledged, with a mandatory expiry WAIVED until <date> (<reason>)

docs.title: Precedence: who wins
docs.text:
The effective knowledge for each subject and kind is computed by one deterministic rule (schemaguru.knowledge.resolve):

  1. Meaning (description, use cases, entity type, pitfalls, glossary): HUMAN beats DRAFTED, always.
  2. Expectations (values, joins, primary keys, soft delete) written by a human or declared by metadata are never replaced by measurement. They are checked; the view shows the expectation and the contradiction ("declared values a,b — observed also c (412 rows)").
  3. Structure (does the column exist, what is its type): the catalog wins; a human note that disagrees is kept and the disagreement is shown.
  4. Among measured facts, the newest wins; the worst verdict wins for warnings.
  5. Drafts are shown with a (draft) marker unless their checkable part was verified.

docs.title: Joins have a direction
docs.text:
A JOIN fact is directed child → parent (orders.customer_id → customers.customer_id) and measured both ways in one probe:

  • match rate — the share of distinct child keys found in the parent (forward);
  • coverage — the share of distinct parent keys reached by the child (reverse);
  • fan-in — child rows per parent key; cardinality N:1, 1:1, 1:N or N:M;
  • verdict — OK (match ≥ 95%), WEAK (≥ 5%) or BROKEN (below 5%; refused).

A join can be perfect forward and nearly empty backward (in the shop, payments → orders matches 100% but covers 5% of orders); the two are different facts and are never mixed.

docs.title: Lazy and read-only
docs.text:
Nothing about an agent's question writes knowledge or spends warehouse money by default. Measurement, drafting and refresh are explicit runs; the question path only queues what it found unmeasured. See Measure and Security.

guru.close()

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
No configuration file is required; every default below is the documented behaviour. sg.Config is a tree of frozen dataclasses. Build it in code, from a mapping, from YAML, or from environment variables — all four give the same object.

import schemaguru as sg

cfg = sg.Config(
    budget=sg.Budget(max_bytes_total=5 << 30),
    sampling=sg.SamplingConfig(llm_values="masked", per_glob={"shop.customers": "none"}),
    graph=sg.GraphConfig(attribution_fanin=20.0),
    measure_on_demand="queue",
)
same = sg.Config.from_mapping({
    "budget": {"max_bytes_total": 5 << 30},
    "sampling": {"llm_values": "masked", "per_glob": {"shop.customers": "none"}},
    "graph": {"attribution_fanin": 20.0},
})
print(cfg == same)

env = sg.Config.from_env(environ={
    "SCHEMAGURU_BUDGET__MAX_BYTES_TOTAL": "5368709120",
    "SCHEMAGURU_GRAPH__ATTRIBUTION_FANIN": "20",
    "SCHEMAGURU_MEASURE_ON_DEMAND": "background",
})
print(env.budget.max_bytes_total, env.graph.attribution_fanin, env.measure_on_demand)

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", config=cfg)
guru.config = sg.Config(agent_checks="allow")    # switch at runtime (stops/restarts the drainer)
guru.close()
  • PREFIX_FIELD sets a top-level field, PREFIX_SECTION__FIELD a nested one; values are parsed as YAML scalars. Tuple fields take a list or comma-separated text.
  • Config.from_yaml("schemaguru.config.yaml") reads the same keys; schemaguru init writes a commented one. The CLI reads --config, else the environment.
  • An unknown key or a value of the wrong type raises ConfigError naming the key. From the environment, only names whose first part is a config field are read (SCHEMAGURU_SCOPE__TYPO still raises): other variables that share the prefix (SCHEMAGURU_URL, SCHEMAGURU_SERVER_TOKENS, SCHEMAGURU_LINEAGE_MEMORY_LIMIT, ...) belong to other parts of SchemaGuru and are ignored.
