docs.title: Cost and scale
docs.text: SchemaGuru is designed for warehouses with hundreds of thousands of tables, where a full scan is unaffordable and a schema dump does not fit in any prompt.

docs.title: Where money is spent
docs.text:
Activity Reads Cost control Crawl system catalog only paged, incremental; queries counted, BigQuery metadata bytes admitted against Budget.crawl_bytes (stops resumably with SG110; readers reporting no bytes are uncounted) Measurement data, through FactLang probes priced before running; max_bytes_per_probe (1 GiB), max_bytes_total (10 GiB per run), max_probes, max_seconds; large tables sampled Agent questions the store only never spend by default (measure_on_demand="queue") check_fact data, one claim off by default; when allowed, admitted through a per-period budget (period_s, 1 day) shared with the background drainer Drafting an LLM draft_budget_tokens; token usage recorded per call

A probe of unknown cost is charged pessimistically (at the per-probe limit) rather than as free, and a probe whose bytes the warehouse does not report is recorded as unknown spend, never as 0. Every spend lands in the store's budget ledger.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
cheap = sg.Budget(max_bytes_per_probe=256 << 20, max_bytes_total=1 << 30, max_seconds=30)
report = guru.measure(all=True, budget=cheap)
print(report.bytes, "bytes,", len(report.measured_tables), "tables,",
      len(report.over_budget), "over budget,", report.unknown_cost_probes, "of unknown cost")
guru.close()

docs.title: Warehouse-specific notes
docs.text:
• BigQuery bills INFORMATION_SCHEMA queries (at least 10 MB each); readers batch per dataset. It bills columns, not rows: key-hash sampling still scans key columns in full, and top values on a huge table may be over budget (SG301).
  • Snowflake uses warehouse compute for metadata and probes.
  • Row counts come from catalog statistics where the reader provides them; otherwise an exact COUNT(*) within budget.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
• Crawl: metadata-only, paged (1,000 tables per page), columns batched (200 tables per query), resumable from a checkpoint, incremental where the warehouse can list changes; memory is bounded by the page size.
  • Search: runs inside the store's full-text index (SQLite FTS5 or Postgres tsvector).
  • Graph: built from join facts once per knowledge change and cached; path search is Dijkstra with a hop limit.
  • Views: an LRU cache (256 views) keyed on snapshot, question and configuration.

Measured on the developer's machine — hardware-dependent, synthetic data:

Benchmark Result Where lexical table search, 50,000-table store p95 ≈ 17 ms tests/benchmark/test_search_latency.py lexical table search, 500,000-table store p95 ≈ 167 ms (store build 23 s) tests/benchmark/test_search_latency.py (-m benchmark) graph expansion, 50,000 joins / 19,800 tables median ≈ 0.48 s benchmarks/bench_expand.py

The search benchmark uses a deliberately dense vocabulary (one word matches about a third of all tables), a worst case. Run them on your own hardware before relying on a number.

The full-size run (500,000 tables, 25,000,000 columns: crawl, incremental crawl, context, join paths and lineage), its targets, the nightly regression workflow and the known limits are on the Scale page.

docs.title: Crawl the catalog
docs.text:
A crawl reads the warehouse's system catalog only — schemas, tables, columns, types, declared keys, comments and statistics — and writes it to the store. It never reads a data row.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", crawl=False)
report = guru.crawl(include=["shop.*"], exclude=["shop.*_t"])
print(report.tables_seen, "seen,", report.tables_written, "written,", report.withdrawn, "withdrawn")
print(report.queries, "metadata queries in", round(report.duration_s, 2), "s")
print(sorted(t.ref.canonical() for t in guru.store.iter_tables()))
for d in report.errors:
    print(d.code, d.message)
guru.close()

docs.title: How it scales
docs.text:
• Paged and streaming. Schemas, then tables in pages (CrawlConfig.page_size, default 1,000); columns and constraints are fetched in batches (column_batch, default 200 tables per query) by up to workers threads (default 4), each query with a timeout (timeout_s, default 60). Each page is written before the next is read, so memory is bounded by the page size, not the warehouse.
  • Resumable. Progress is checkpointed after every page; an interrupted crawl continues from its checkpoint. Schemas listed before the checkpoint are skipped unless the store has never seen them (created since the interruption); a checkpoint saved under a different include/exclude scope is discarded and the crawl starts from the top.
  • Incremental. When the reader can list "changed since" (last_altered), a later crawl re-reads only changed tables, plus a name-only listing per schema to detect drops. A change of the include/exclude scope makes the next crawl a full one.
  • Withdrawn, not deleted. A table missing from a complete listing is marked withdrawn; its facts are kept for one refresh cycle and reported as drift. Human overlays on it are never deleted.
  • Failure isolation. A schema, page or batch that fails is skipped and reported (SG102); the crawl continues.

docs.title: Scope filters
docs.text:
include and exclude are case-sensitive globs matched against schema.table and catalog.schema.table. An empty include allows everything; exclude wins. The defaults exclude information_schema.*, pg_catalog.*, sys.*, *.*_staging* and *.*tmp*. Excluded objects are never stored. Set them for every crawl in Config(crawl=...):

cfg = sg.Config(crawl=sg.CrawlConfig(include=("shop.*",), page_size=500))
print(cfg.crawl.exclude)

docs.title: Readers
docs.text:
One reader per dialect, each reading only that warehouse's system views with bind parameters for every value; the metadata SQL is the only SQL SchemaGuru writes.

Dialect Reads Validated DuckDB duckdb_tables(), duckdb_columns(), duckdb_constraints() real engine, CI PostgreSQL pg_catalog (row estimates from reltuples, comments from pg_description) real engine, CI MySQL / MariaDB information_schema real engine, CI ClickHouse system.tables, system.columns (no foreign keys) real engine, CI SQL Server sys.* views, MS_Description comments real engine, CI Trino <catalog>.information_schema.* (constraints usually absent) real engine, CI BigQuery region-*.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.* (billed: admitted against Budget.crawl_bytes) recorded metadata only Snowflake <db>.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.*, SHOW … KEYS recorded metadata only Redshift SVV_* views, pg_constraint recorded metadata only Databricks Unity Catalog system.information_schema.* recorded metadata only Oracle ALL_* dictionary views recorded metadata only

The ClickHouse, DuckDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Trino readers are tested against real engines in CI. The BigQuery, Databricks, Oracle, Redshift and Snowflake readers are built from the documented system views and tested on recorded metadata, not yet validated against live accounts. Azure Synapse is supported through the SQL Server reader and is not tested in CI.

Known limits: the BigQuery incremental listing misses schema-only changes (a column added without the table's last_altered moving), so run a periodic full crawl (schemaguru.catalog.crawl(guru.reader, guru.store, incremental=False)); Redshift has no incremental listing. Every shipped reader also implements view_definitions (ReaderCapabilities.view_definitions): the crawl reads each view's SQL from the engine's metadata views and parses it into lineage (needs the lineage extra; CrawlReport.views_parsed counts them and lineage_diagnostics carries SG211/SG212). A custom reader that lacks the method is never asked. Per-warehouse permissions and cost notes are in the project wiki's warehouse guides.

A warehouse that is not listed needs a custom reader.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
A full crawl from Python:

from schemaguru.catalog import crawl

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", crawl=False)
print(crawl(guru.reader, guru.store, incremental=False).tables_seen)
guru.close()

Every crawl reports the metadata queries it ran and, where the warehouse bills metadata (BigQuery), the bytes billed (report.bytes_billed; bytes_billed_is_estimate says when it is a lower bound). Budget.crawl_bytes caps those bytes: before each listing query the bytes billed so far in this crawl are compared with it, and once it is reached the crawl stops between pages with warning SG110, keeps its checkpoint, and the next crawl() (or schemaguru crawl) resumes where it stopped. Readers that report no bytes (every warehouse but BigQuery today) are not counted, so the cap never stops them.

docs.title: Drafting with an LLM
docs.text:
Measurement says what is there; it cannot say what it means. Drafting asks an LLM for the meaning — table and column descriptions, the questions a table answers, its entity type, pitfalls, a soft-delete guess, type notes, PII guesses, join candidates and glossary terms — and stores the answer as drafts: DRAFTED facts marked (draft) in every view until a check passes or a person accepts them.

Everything else in SchemaGuru works with no LLM at all.

docs.title: A run
docs.text:
import json

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.draft import CallableProvider


def scripted_llm(system: str, user: str, schema: dict, max_tokens: int) -> dict:
    """Stands in for a model: answers every table it is shown (see the input it gets)."""
    tables = json.loads(user)["tables"]
    return {"tables": [{
        "table": t["table"],
        "description": f"One row per {t['table'].split('.')[-1].rstrip('s')}.",
        "columns": [], "use_cases": ["How many are there per month?"],
        "entity_type": None, "pitfalls": [], "soft_delete": None, "type_notes": [],
        "pii": [], "join_candidates": [], "glossary": [],
    } for t in tables]}


guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
report = guru.draft(["shop.products", "shop.sessions"], provider=CallableProvider(scripted_llm))
print(report.calls, "call(s),", report.tokens, "tokens (estimated:", report.estimated_tokens, ")")
for f in report.drafted:
    print(f.kind.name, f.subject.canonical(), f.status.value, dict(f.value))

Real providers:

from schemaguru.draft import AnthropicProvider, OpenAICompatibleProvider

guru.draft(["analytics.*"], provider=AnthropicProvider())        # model claude-sonnet-5-5
guru.draft(["analytics.*"], provider=OpenAICompatibleProvider(
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key=None, model="my-local-model"))

AnthropicProvider (extra anthropic) asks for structured output through a tool; forcing the tool choice is off by default (force_tool=True turns it on), following the Anthropic API reference for Sonnet 5.5 — this has not been verified live. OpenAICompatibleProvider (extra openai) works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including local servers. CallableProvider(fn) wraps any function; fn may be async and may return (reply, Usage) when it knows the token usage. Writing your own: LLM provider.

docs.title: What the model sees
docs.text:
One call per table (small tables are batched): table and column names, types, comments, catalog statistics, the measured facts (null rates, distinct counts), declared constraints, neighbouring table names — and observed values only as the value policy allows (masked by default; see PII). A final shape sweep runs over every outbound payload in masked mode; hits are masked and counted (report.pii_sweep_hits).

The reply must match a JSON schema (schemaguru.draft.DRAFT_SCHEMA). An invalid reply is retried once; after that the table's draft is an ERROR fact (SG401) — never partially applied. A provider failure costs that call's tables (SG403). draft_budget_tokens (or budget= on the call) caps a run (SG402). Prompts are versioned files in schemaguru/draft/prompts/; their hash is recorded on every drafted fact.

docs.title: Checking drafts
docs.text: Every checkable part of a draft becomes a FactLang claim and is run within budget: a soft-delete predicate (must parse as a safe filter, else SG406, and must leave some rows and exclude some), type notes (PATTERN), join candidates (JOIN), an entity type (UNIQUE on the claimed key). Passing parts become VERIFIED; prose stays a draft. A claim that cannot be checked (no verdict, e.g. FactLang lacks the capability) stays UNVERIFIED (SG405).

docs.title: Accepting drafts
docs.text:
A person turns drafts into HUMAN facts (source accepted:<draft id>); human facts always win over drafts for meaning.

ids = [f.id for f in report.drafted if f.kind.name == "DESCRIPTION"]
accepted = guru.accept(ids, write_overlay="schemaguru/accepted.yaml")
print(len(accepted), "accepted;", open("schemaguru/accepted.yaml", encoding="utf-8").read()[:120])
guru.close()

From the terminal: schemaguru draft 'shop.*', then schemaguru review (walks the drafts: yes / no / edit / skip / quit) or schemaguru accept <ids…>; schemaguru export-drafts writes them to a separate, reviewable YAML file. SchemaGuru never edits a file you wrote: --write-overlay appends to a machine-owned accepted.yaml.

Drafting never runs on an agent's query path; it runs only when you call it.

docs.title: Runtime feedback
docs.text:
When an agent's query fails, the failure says something about the warehouse: a column that is stored as text but compared as a date, a column that does not exist where the agent thought. Tell SchemaGuru, and the next measurement run looks there first.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
sql = "SELECT count(*) FROM shop.orders o WHERE o.created_at > DATE '2025-06-01'"
# a BigQuery-style message: operand types plus the position of the operator
error = (f"No matching signature for operator > for argument types: STRING, DATE "
         f"at [1:{sql.index('>') + 1}]")
print(guru.report_error(sql, error, dialect="bigquery"), "record(s)")
# without a position the failing column cannot be identified: nothing is recorded
print(guru.report_error(sql, "Cannot compare values of type VARCHAR and type DATE"))
guru.report_error("SELECT o.refund_amount FROM shop.orders o",
                  'Binder Error: Table "o" does not have a column named "refund_amount"')
for row in guru.feedback_summary():
    print(row)
guru.close()

report_error(sql, error_message, dialect=None):

  • never raises and never writes facts: it only queues feedback (knowledge is never changed on the agent's query path);
  • stores identifiers and counts only, keyed on (table, column, failure class) — never the SQL text;
  • returns the number of records written.

docs.title: Failure classes
docs.text:
Class Detected from type_mismatch the error's operand types and position (BigQuery at [line:col], PostgreSQL at character N / LINE), resolved to the column at that position in the SQL (aliases resolved, string literals blanked first; numeric-vs-numeric pairs ignored). A message without a position records nothing unknown_column "no such column" errors, resolved through aliases unknown_table "no such table" errors ambiguous_column "ambiguous column" errors

Each is a plug-in FailureClassifier; add your own.

docs.title: Effect
docs.text:
Feedback raises the table's measurement priority (guru.measure(all=True) measures the hottest tables first) and, for unknown_*, triggers a targeted re-crawl of the table at the next refresh. guru.feedback_summary() lists the hot spots, including those no fact covers yet.

For refusing unsafe SQL before it runs, see the read-only guard helper in Security.

docs.title: Join graph and path search
docs.text:
guru.find_path(a, b) answers "how do I join these two tables?" from measured joins only. It returns up to k routes with their join keys and weakest support, or a typed refusal that names what blocks the route. It never returns a join it has not measured (unless you opt in to unmeasured candidates).

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure(all=True)

result = guru.find_path("shop.payments", "shop.customers")
for path in result.paths:
    print(" -> ".join(t.canonical() for t in path.tables),
          "coverage", path.coverage, "provisional" if path.provisional else "")
for a, b in [("shop.orders", "shop.events"), ("shop.orders", "shop.orders")]:
    r = guru.find_path(a, b)
    print(r.refusal.value, "-", r.explanation)

docs.title: Edges
docs.text: One edge per measured JOIN fact with verdict OK (match ≥ 95%) or WEAK (≥ 5%). BROKEN joins and joins to missing objects are refused, not discounted. Unmeasured candidates enter only with GraphConfig(include_unmeasured=True), at a penalty. A malformed fact costs one edge (SG601), never the graph.

docs.title: Cost of a hop
docs.text:
Lower is better; costs add along a route:

cost(hop) = w_support * -ln(support in the traversed direction)
          + w_fanout  * ln(1 + distinct_left)
          + w_hub     * ln(1 + in_degree(arrival table))

Support is the match rate child → parent and the coverage parent → child. Defaults: w_support=1.0, w_fanout=0.35, w_hub=0.25, unmeasured_penalty=1.0 (used in place of the support term when support is unknown); support 0 is never traversed. An unknown fan-out is priced at the graph's worst known one, so unknown is never cheaper than known.

The fan-out term is a weak proxy

In the system SchemaGuru's design descends from, ln(1 + distinct_left) correlated only −0.30 with the true rows per key. It stays because nothing measured replaces it yet. All weights are read from GraphConfig at call time, so you can sweep them.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
• Dijkstra over both directions of every edge (SQL joins are symmetric), at most hop_limit (6) hops; the hop count is part of the search state, so a cheap long route cannot hide a short one.
  • k_paths (3) best routes by Yen's algorithm.
  • Thin support is a preference, not a ban. A first pass avoids any hop with support below thin_support (5%); a second pass allows them. Second-pass routes are appended after the first-pass ones and marked provisional with their narrowest support, so a thin but correct direct join is still offered — labelled.
  • Path.coverage is the narrowest support over the hops, None when any hop is unknown; Path.estimated marks numbers from a sample.

docs.title: The hub guard
docs.text:
Two joins can each be right and still multiply rows together. In the shop, orders and events both point at accounts many-to-one; joining orders → accounts → events pairs every order with every event of its account. The join-paths part of guru.context("events per account and session"):

Join paths (join keys, advisory; support = the weakest hop's match or coverage):
  ⚠ no safe route (shop.events -> shop.orders; shop.sessions -> shop.orders): every route pivots through hub shop.accounts on two attribution edges (fan-in > 10): a cartesian hazard
  shop.events → shop.sessions · support 100%
    events.session_id = sessions.session_id (N:1)
  shop.events → shop.accounts · support 100%
    events.account_id = accounts.account_id (N:1)
  shop.accounts → shop.orders · support 40%
    orders.account_id = accounts.account_id (N:1)
  • An edge is an attribution edge when its fan-in (child rows per parent key) exceeds attribution_fanin (10.0).
  • A hub is a table that only receives edges and either has an ENTITY_TYPE fact or is reached by attribution edges from at least two distinct tables — measured shape alone, so the guard works with no LLM and no overlay.
  • The refused shape is arriving at a hub on an attribution edge and leaving on another (HUB_PIVOT). The hub itself is not banned: routes that start or end there are fine.

The default threshold is a judgement call. calibrate_hubs reports the fan-ins into each hub and proposes the centre of the widest gap; accept it into GraphConfig yourself:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

from schemaguru.graph import build_edges, calibrate_hubs
from schemaguru.knowledge import resolve

effective = resolve(guru.store.facts_for(None, ["JOIN"]), now=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
                    ttl_days=guru.config.fact_ttl_days)
for c in calibrate_hubs(build_edges(effective, cfg=guru.config.graph)):
    print(c.hub.canonical(), c.fan_ins, c.proposed_threshold)

docs.title: Typed refusals
docs.text:
Refusal Meaning NO_EVIDENCE no usable measured join touches one of the tables SAME_TABLE both ends are the same table NO_ROUTE measured joins exist, but no chain of them connects the tables within the hop limit WAYPOINT_UNSATISFIABLE a waypoint rule for this pair can never be met RULE_REJECTS_ALL routes exist, but every one breaks a waypoint rule HUB_PIVOT every route pivots through a hub on two attribution edges

To say why, the search re-runs with exactly one mechanism relaxed; the relaxed route is never returned as a path.

docs.title: Waypoint rules
docs.text:
People can constrain routes in an overlay: a pair rule may require and forbid, a node rule may only forbid (a table as an intermediate step). Predicates are node(t), col(t.c), edge(a.x->b.y) and any, matched exactly; every rule needs a because:.

waypoints:
  - pair: [shop.events, shop.orders]
    require: "edge(shop.events.session_id->shop.sessions.session_id)"
    because: events link to orders only through sessions
  - node: shop.accounts
    because: accounts is an attribution hub, never a bridge

A malformed rule refuses the searches it governs (SG602, fail closed); more than 16 requirements is SG603; a requirement that matches nothing is a lint warning (SG604). Identity chains (chains: in an overlay) compile into pair rules; a chain that cannot be compiled is reported (SG605), never dropped silently.

docs.title: SQL join snippets
docs.text:
Each path can render a dialect-correct FROM … JOIN … ON … snippet (casts, composite keys, the tables' soft-delete predicates) through FactLang's render_join. It is advice for the agent; SchemaGuru never executes it. With a FactLang that lacks render_join the path is shown with its join keys only (SG501).

print(guru.handle_tool_call("find_join_path", {"from": "payments", "to": "customers"})["text"])
guru.close()

docs.title: Lineage
docs.text:
What a table or column is built from, and what reads it: analytics.revenue_daily is made from shop.orders and shop.refunds; its net_revenue column comes from orders.amount. SchemaGuru reads lineage from three places, stores it as two fact kinds (LINEAGE per table, COLUMN_LINEAGE per column), and hands it to agents through the lineage tool and one extra line per table in the view.

Lineage is declared or parsed, never measured and never verified: every lineage fact is UNVERIFIED, and no resolver step promotes it. It answers "where does this come from", not "how do I join these". It is never a join path: two tables built from the same source are not thereby joinable, and find_join_path does not read lineage.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Source Provenance What it gives dbt manifest (import_dbt) DECLARED, source dbt:manifest:<id> table lineage from depends_on.nodes; column lineage from compiled_code View definitions (the crawl) CATALOG, source view_definition table and column lineage parsed from the view's SQL Overlays HUMAN, source overlay:<file>:<line> what a person says, which always beats a parsed link

dbt. guru.import_dbt("target/manifest.json") writes a LINEAGE fact for every model, snapshot or seed whose relation is in the store, from depends_on.nodes mapped to relations (sources and refs; tests, macros and metrics are not relations, and an ephemeral model's own inputs are inherited by its consumers). Column lineage is parsed from each node's compiled_code with the node's adapter dialect. A manifest that was never compiled has no compiled_code: only table-level lineage is imported, with one SG214 per import (run dbt compile). Re-importing retracts the lineage facts the new manifest no longer produces. Two nodes that write one relation from the same inputs but with different details are SG215; the first by node id is kept.

View definitions. A reader that can read definitions reports view_definitions=True in its ReaderCapabilities, and the crawl parses every view it writes (or re-reads) into lineage. The sources, all metadata views and never a data table:

Warehouse Where the definition comes from PostgreSQL pg_views.definition, pg_matviews.definition Redshift pg_views.definition (the current database only: datashares are not listed) DuckDB duckdb_views().sql Snowflake INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS.VIEW_DEFINITION BigQuery INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS, INFORMATION_SCHEMA.MATERIALIZED_VIEWS Databricks information_schema.views.view_definition MySQL / MariaDB information_schema.VIEWS.VIEW_DEFINITION ClickHouse system.tables.as_select SQL Server / Synapse sys.sql_modules.definition Oracle ALL_VIEWS.TEXT, ALL_MVIEWS.QUERY Trino information_schema.views.view_definition

A custom catalog reader that does not implement view_definitions keeps working; the crawl never asks it. A view is not parsed again while its definition is unchanged (same sha256) and the relation names it reads still resolve as they did (same stored relation, same columns). An upstream table entering the crawl's scope, leaving it, or gaining or losing a column re-parses the view, so (not in catalog) and SELECT * lineage catch up. A re-crawled view's lineage is replaced in one transaction, and a dropped view's lineage goes with it.

docs.title: The lineage extra
docs.text:
pip install 'schemaguru[lineage]'     # sqlglot, used to parse SQL

Without it, nothing is parsed from SQL: a crawl does not even read the view definitions and reports SG212 (once per crawl or import); the dbt import still writes table-level lineage from depends_on, but no column lineage. Overlay lineage needs no parser. So view lineage of any level, and every column-level link parsed from SQL, needs the extra.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
import duckdb
import schemaguru as sg

con = duckdb.connect("warehouse.duckdb")
con.execute("CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS analytics")
con.execute("""CREATE VIEW analytics.paid_orders AS
               SELECT order_id, customer_id, CAST(order_id AS BIGINT) AS order_no
               FROM shop.orders WHERE status = 'paid'""")
con.execute("""CREATE VIEW analytics.paid_by_customer AS
               SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS paid_orders
               FROM analytics.paid_orders GROUP BY customer_id""")
con.close()

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", crawl=True)
print(guru.handle_tool_call("lineage", {"ref": "analytics.paid_by_customer", "depth": 2})["text"])
print(guru.handle_tool_call("lineage", {"ref": "shop.orders", "direction": "downstream"})["text"])
result = guru.lineage("analytics.paid_orders.order_no")
print([(e.downstream, e.upstream, e.transform) for e in result.edges])

Lineage upstream of analytics.paid_by_customer (table level, depth 2) — declared/parsed, unverified; not a join path
  analytics.paid_by_customer <- analytics.paid_orders [view_definition]
  analytics.paid_orders <- shop.orders [view_definition]
Lineage downstream of shop.orders (table level, depth 2) — declared/parsed, unverified; not a join path
  analytics.paid_orders <- shop.orders [view_definition]
  analytics.paid_by_customer <- analytics.paid_orders [view_definition]
[('analytics.paid_orders.order_no', 'shop.orders.order_id', 'cast')]

The same from a shell: schemaguru lineage analytics.paid_by_customer [--downstream] [--depth N] [--level table|column] [--format text|json]; over HTTP, GET /lineage?ref=…&direction=…&depth=…&level=… (server mode). guru.lineage(...) returns a LineageResult (it has no __str__; use the tool's text, or read its nodes, edges, truncated and cycles). depth is 1 to 5, a walk stops at 200 nodes (truncated), and a cycle (possible with a mis-declared dbt graph or overlay) is reported, never followed.

docs.title: Overlay syntax
docs.text:
lineage:
  - table: analytics.revenue_daily
    upstream: [shop.orders, shop.refunds]
  - column: analytics.revenue_daily.net_revenue
    inputs: [shop.orders.amount, shop.refunds.amount]
    transform: aggregate
  - table: analytics.legacy_view
    upstream: [shop.orders]
    ignore: true          # hides this parsed link; human always wins
  • A human entry with a list replaces every parsed link (dbt and view) of that subject and level; table and column levels are independent.
  • ignore: true without a list hides every parsed link of that level for the subject; with a list it hides only a parsed link whose sorted list is exactly that list. An ignore that hides nothing is SG213: usually the view was redefined and the new link is the one shown.
  • Hidden facts stay in the store (explain shows them) and return when the entry is removed.
  • Without a human entry, dbt and view links are both effective: identical lists render as one line naming both sources, differing lists once each.

transform is copy (a bare column), cast, expression, aggregate, window or unknown. The full rules are on the overlays page.

docs.title: What agents see
docs.text:
• agent profile. After the description, Built from: <ref>, <ref> (+N more) · <source> · unverified; per column that has lineage, ← <input>[, <input>] (<transform>), at most 3 inputs then +N more. An input the store does not hold reads <name> (not in catalog). The provenance footer names the lineage source and says unverified.
  • planner profile. The table-level line only. router: unchanged.
  • verifier profile. Keyed lines, one per distinct link (so one table can carry several LINEAGE lines): LINEAGE <table> <- <ref>[, <ref>…] and COLUMN_LINEAGE <table>.<column> <- <ref>[, <ref>…] <transform>, an unresolved ref written name(unresolved) with no space.
  • The lineage tool, in the tool list of Python, the CLI, HTTP, MCP and the framework adapters: arguments ref, direction (upstream default or downstream), depth (1 to 5, default 2), level (table or column, default the level of ref). It returns JSON with text, nodes, edges (each with its sources and transform), truncated and cycles. The prompt block tells the agent it is declared or parsed, never measured, and never a join path.

Lineage never adds a table to a scoped view by itself: scoping stays question-driven. When a model and one of its direct upstream tables are both in the view, the model's block shows Built from.

docs.title: Privacy of view SQL
docs.text: The raw definition text exists in memory only while it is parsed. The store keeps the lineage facts, the sha256 of the definition and the relation names it reads (to skip an unchanged view next time) and, as evidence, a template with every literal replaced by a placeholder. Where the dialect reads "..." as a string (BigQuery, Databricks/Spark, Hive, MySQL/MariaDB, T-SQL, SQLite, and any dialect SchemaGuru does not know) every "..." span is blanked too; only in ANSI-quoting dialects (Postgres, Snowflake, DuckDB, Trino, Redshift, Oracle, ClickHouse, ...) is a "quoted identifier" kept. No raw definition is persisted, logged, rendered, put in a diagnostic or sent to an LLM; a diagnostic names a fixed failure category, never SQL text.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A definition over 1,000,000 characters is skipped before parsing (SG211 too_large).
  • Parsing runs in a reused worker process (a fresh python -m schemaguru.lineage.worker process, like the spawn start method, on every OS) with a hard 5 s cap per request; a definition takes two requests (extract its tables, then the lineage), so the cap is per request, not per definition. A timeout kills the worker, replaces it and gives that definition SG211 timeout and no lineage; a worker that dies is SG211 worker_died. A worker survives a hard-killed parent only until its current parse returns (at most the 5 s cap).
  • The worker has a 1 GiB address-space cap on Linux only; on other systems only the 5 s cap applies.
  • The worker is started as sys.executable -m schemaguru.lineage.worker. Where sys.executable is not a Python that can import SchemaGuru (an embedded interpreter, a frozen app, or a sys.path extended only at runtime that the child does not inherit), every view fails closed with SG211 worker_died and gets no lineage; the rest of the crawl is unaffected.
  • When the reader's view_definitions call itself fails (SG102), the views of that batch keep the lineage of their last successful parse: a transient error must not drop lineage. A view the reader answers without a definition is different: its lineage is retracted (SG211 definition_unavailable).
  • SELECT * and unqualified columns are expanded with the columns the store holds; a name it does not hold is listed as unresolved, never guessed.
  • Projection lineage only: a column used only in WHERE, JOIN ON or GROUP BY is not an input.
  • An unaliased computed output (a bare SUM(x)) gets no column lineage.
  • A deleted JOIN edge can stay in the cached join graph until the snapshot, generation or date changes; lineage itself is not affected.
  • Lineage is never a join path and never VERIFIED; a dbt or overlay link says what a person or a tool declared, and a parsed link says what the SQL text says, not what the data does.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Code Meaning SG211 a definition could not be parsed (parse_error, too_large, timeout, unsupported_dialect, worker_died) SG212 column-level lineage needs the lineage extra SG213 a lineage ignore entry matches no parsed link SG214 the dbt manifest has no compiled_code: table-level lineage only SG705 the store has no lineage index (a custom store): downstream lineage is unavailable

SG215 (two dbt nodes write one relation with different details) is listed in the diagnostics reference with the rest.

Lineage at 500,000 tables is measured on the Scale page.

docs.title: Measure
docs.text:
Measurement turns guesses into numbers. Every number comes from a read-only FactLang probe — SchemaGuru never writes measurement SQL itself — and is stored with its method and time.

Runs through FactLang

The probes run through FactLang's Checker.measure (FactLang 0.1.4 or later). With a FactLang that lacks it, measure() returns SG304 and writes nothing. The generated outputs on this site use the test suite's backend so that they are reproducible byte for byte.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
Probe (FactLang) Fact Notes row count (ROWS, or catalog statistics) ROW_COUNT never sampled non-null and distinct counts, fused per table NULL_RATE, DISTINCT an empty table is UNMEASURABLE; an all-null column is a dead column (NULL_RATE = 1.0) top observed values, when distinct ≤ enum_max_distinct (20) VALUES (observed, with counts) exact top-k, never random rows declared values (VALUES … IN [...]) VALUES status the human list is checked, never edited key uniqueness (UNIQUE, composite keys in full) PRIMARY_KEY status joins, both directions (KeyOverlap) JOIN match rate, coverage, row match, fan-in, cardinality, verdict string patterns (PATTERN … LIKE) TYPE_NOTE e.g. ISO dates or epoch numbers stored as text freshness (FRESH) on timestamp columns FRESHNESS never sampled 
import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
report = guru.measure(["shop.orders", "shop.customers"])
print([t.canonical() for t in report.measured_tables], report.facts_written, "facts")
print("checks:", sorted(report.checks_run))

join = next(
    f for f in guru.store.facts_for(None, ["JOIN"])
    if f.subject.left[0].table == "orders" and f.subject.left[0].column == "customer_id"
)
v = join.value
print(v["match_rate"], v["coverage"], v["cardinality"], v["verdict"], join.method)

Rates are stored unrounded; views round them (four significant digits).

docs.title: Which joins are measured
docs.text: A join is measured only if it is a candidate, in this order: declared foreign keys from the catalog; joins from overlays and dbt relationships tests; name and type heuristics (x_id, xId, x_fk → a table x or xs with a compatible key; a column named like another table's single-column primary key in the same schema; at most 5 per column, same catalog only); and joins an LLM draft suggested. A candidate is never shown as a join until it is measured. Keys of different type families (text vs integer) are measured with a cast and flagged, because the agent must cast too.

docs.title: Lazy by default
docs.text:
An agent's question never spends warehouse money by itself (Config.measure_on_demand):

Mode What context() does with an unmeasured table it shows queue (default) marks it unmeasured and puts it on the queue; nothing runs background the same, and one daemon thread drains the queue under the budget block measures the scoped tables before answering, at most block_timeout_s (10 s)

The queue is drained by guru.measure() (no targets) or guru.measure_queue(), guru.refresh(), or schemaguru worker.

lazy = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb", store=".schemaguru/lazy.db")
lazy.context("events per account and session")          # queues what it showed
print(lazy.measure_queue().measured_tables)              # an explicit spend
lazy.close()

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
Every probe is priced first (a dry run where the warehouse supports one; otherwise catalog bytes, labelled heuristic). sg.Budget:

Field Default Effect max_bytes_per_probe 1 GiB a probe over it is not run: fact ERROR over_budget (SG301) max_bytes_total 10 GiB when spent, the run stops and the rest stays queued (SG302) max_probes, max_seconds none further caps per run period_s 1 day a budget shared across runs (the background drainer, agent checks) refills once per period

A probe whose cost is unknown is charged pessimistically (at the per-probe limit) and, if the warehouse reports no bytes either, recorded as unknown spend, never as 0. Every byte goes to the store's budget ledger.

small = guru.measure("shop.events", budget=sg.Budget(max_bytes_total=64 << 20, max_probes=20))
print(small.bytes, "bytes;", small.unknown_cost_probes, "probes of unknown cost;",
      [t.canonical() for t in small.over_budget], "over budget")
guru.close()

docs.title: Failure is local
docs.text:
A probe that fails produces an ERROR fact for that subject only (SG303); the run goes on. Asking to measure a table that was never crawled is SG305.

See also: Sampling large tables · Cost and scale.

docs.title: Overlays (human YAML)
docs.text: An overlay is where people write what the data cannot say: what a table means, which values a column should take, how to find live rows, which joins to trust, what a business term means. Overlays are plain YAML — reviewable in pull requests, diffable, owned by people. SchemaGuru never edits a file you wrote.

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
One schemaguru.yaml, or a directory schemaguru/*.yaml. This is the complete example the test suite loads (spec §14.1):

version: 1
warehouse: shop
tables:
  shop.orders:
    description: One row per order placed on the storefront.
    use_cases: [revenue by month, average basket size]
    entity_type: order
    soft_delete: "deleted IS NULL OR NOT deleted"
    pitfalls:
      - rule: Refunds are a second row with negative amount.
        fix: Filter amount > 0 for gross revenue.
    columns:
      status:
        description: Payment state of the order.
        values: [paid, refunded, cancelled]      # an expectation: checked, never auto-edited
        values_split: ":"                        # optional
      created_at:
        type_note: ISO-8601 timestamp stored as STRING
    joins:
      - to: shop.customers.customer_id
        from: customer_id
        cardinality: N:1
chains:
  - name: order to payment provider
    because: payments are matched via the order reference, not the customer
    steps: [shop.orders.order_id -> shop.payments.order_id]
waypoints:
  - pair: [shop.events, shop.orders]
    require: "edge(shop.events.session_id->shop.sessions.session_id)"
    because: events link to orders only through sessions (measured 0% direct match)
glossary:
  - term: active customer
    definition: ordered in the last 90 days
    maps_to: [shop.orders, shop.customers]
never_query:
  - table: shop.orders_backup_2019
    reason: frozen copy, not maintained
waivers:
  - fact: "VALUES shop.orders.status"
    reason: legacy upper-case rows being migrated
    expires: 2027-01-31
Section Holds Becomes tables.<t>.description, use_cases, entity_type, pitfalls meaning HUMAN facts that always beat drafts tables.<t>.columns.<c>.values (+ values_split) an expected enum an expectation: checked, never edited; contradictions shown tables.<t>.soft_delete a FactLang filter giving the live rows a SOFT_DELETE expectation tables.<t>.columns.<c>.type_note how a column is really stored a note shown next to the measured type tables.<t>.joins a join you vouch for (to, from, cardinality, cast_to) a JOIN expectation (a candidate to measure) chains a join recipe, steps of joins, filters and notes, with because compiled into a waypoint rule waypoints route rules for path search (graph) rules glossary term, definition, maps_to tables glossary facts; their tables join the scope when the term is asked about never_query tables agents must not use, with a reason listed in every view; sg.guard.check_sql(..., never_query=...) refuses SQL reading them waivers an acknowledged contradiction, with reason and a mandatory expires WAIVED until the date lineage where a table or column comes from: table + upstream, or column + inputs + transform; ignore: true hides parsed links LINEAGE / COLUMN_LINEAGE facts, human-written; see Lineage entries

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure("shop.orders")
for d in guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml"):
    print(d.code, d.severity.value, d.location, d.message)
print(guru.context("refund rate by month").text)
guru.close()
  • It never raises on data. Every problem is a diagnostic with file:line: unsupported version (SG201), an unknown key with a close-match suggestion (SG202), a reference to nothing in the store (SG203) or to several things (SG204, candidates listed), an invalid filter (SG205), a waiver without a valid expires (SG206) or already expired (SG207), a malformed entry (SG208). An empty key counts as absent.
  • One call, all files. Each load_overlays call replaces the previously loaded rules, chains, waivers and overlay facts. Pass every overlay path in one call: guru.load_overlays("schemaguru/", "team-a.yaml"). An entry you delete from a file (or a file you no longer pass) has its facts retracted from the store, and so does an entry with an error of its own (an SG208 on that entry retracts that entry's previous fact; the rest of the file loads). A file that fails as a whole (unreadable, not YAML, not a mapping, unsupported version) keeps its previous facts until it loads again.
  • What persists. The HUMAN facts (descriptions, expectations, glossary, …) are written to the store. Waypoint rules, chains and waivers live on the Guru that loaded them; load the overlays in the process that serves the agent.
  • Filters (soft delete, chain filters) are checked with FactLang's parser; with a FactLang that lacks it, syntax only (SG503, informational). In SQL snippets SchemaGuru quotes a soft-delete column in the catalog's exact case; when two columns differ only in case, the exact spelling wins, and a name matching several of them stays unquoted (SG506).
  • A soft-delete filter is checked against the data. It must name existing columns and, when it compares one column with values, at least one of them must occur in that column's measured values (TRUE/FALSE need a boolean column; NULLs are always fine). A mismatch is SG210: the view warns and SQL snippets leave the filter out. The text is never edited.

Lint overlays in CI without touching your store — it loads them into a throwaway copy and exits 1 on findings:

schemaguru lint schemaguru.yaml schemaguru/

The CLI and overlays in 0.1

In 0.1 only schemaguru lint reads overlay files. The other commands (context, path, mcp, …) serve what is in the store, so load overlays from Python (guru.load_overlays(...)) to put their facts there.

docs.title: Expectations are alarms
docs.text:
A declared enum, join, key or soft-delete rule is never "corrected" to match the data. When measurement disagrees, both are shown and the disagreement is a warning:

WHERE status = 'paid' counts 5,000 orders; 5,412 are paid. The overlay declares paid, refunded, cancelled; measurement found PAID as well. SchemaGuru keeps the human expectation and states the contradiction (here under a waiver with an expiry date):

  ⚠ WAIVED until 2027-01-31 (legacy upper-case rows being migrated): status: declared values 'paid','refunded','cancelled' — observed also 'PAID' (412 rows)
  ⚠ status: case drift: 'paid'/'PAID' differ only in case — compare case-insensitively
    status       VARCHAR  values: 'paid','refunded','cancelled' (+ observed 'PAID'); distinct 4 (measured 2026-11-24); Payment state of the order.

Acknowledge a known contradiction with a waiver; it expires, and an expired waiver is ignored and reported.

docs.title: Drafts and accepted drafts
docs.text: LLM drafts never go into your files. schemaguru export-drafts schemaguru/drafts.yaml writes them to a separate, generated file for review; schemaguru accept <ids> (or review) stores accepted drafts as HUMAN facts and, with --write-overlay, appends them to a machine-owned schemaguru/accepted.yaml.

docs.title: dbt
docs.text: schemaguru import-dbt target/manifest.json (or sg.overlays.import_dbt(path, guru.store)) maps model and column descriptions to DECLARED descriptions, relationships tests to joins, accepted_values to expected values, and a single unique + not_null column to a primary key — all DECLARED, UNVERIFIED until measured. Only models and columns present in the store are mapped; an unreadable manifest is SG209.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Loading never raises on data; every problem is a line-numbered diagnostic and the entry is skipped. A key written twice in one mapping is SG208 naming both lines, and neither entry is applied. A waiver's fact must start with a registered fact kind (SG208 otherwise) and its subject glob should match something in the store (SG203, a warning: the waiver still loads but can never apply). Glossary maps_to takes tables only; a column is SG203.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• A malformed overlay entry's previous facts are retracted on the next load: fix the entry and reload. (A file that fails as a whole, unreadable or not YAML, keeps its previous facts.)
  • Join entries in an overlay are declarations. They carry a cardinality you vouch for and nothing else; measured numbers (match rate, coverage) come only from measurement, never from a human or a dbt file.
  • export-drafts and accept --write-overlay write only kinds that have an overlay form; the others are left out and named in a warning (and printed by export-drafts).

docs.title: Lineage entries
docs.text:
Where lineage comes from, what agents see and its limits: Lineage.

lineage:
  - table: analytics.revenue_daily
    upstream: [shop.orders, shop.refunds]
  - column: analytics.revenue_daily.net_revenue
    inputs: [shop.orders.amount, shop.refunds.amount]
    transform: aggregate        # copy | cast | expression | aggregate | window | unknown (default)
  - table: analytics.legacy_view
    upstream: [shop.orders]
    ignore: true                # hides this parsed link; human always wins

Each entry is one human fact (source overlay:<file>:<line>). Exactly one of table / column; upstream goes with table, inputs with column; every name must resolve (SG203 / SG204 drop the entry); a non-ignore entry needs a non-empty list; a malformed entry is SG208.

  • A human entry with a list replaces every parsed link (view definition, dbt) of that subject and level. Table and column levels are independent.
  • ignore: true without a list hides all parsed links of that level for the subject; with a list it hides only a parsed link whose sorted list is exactly equal. Hidden facts stay in the store (explain shows them) and return when the entry is removed.
  • An ignore that hides nothing is SG213 (a warning, reported by load_overlays and schemaguru lint): typically the view was redefined after the ignore was written, so its old link is gone and the new one is shown. Update the ignore to the new list or drop it.
  • Two identical lines are one fact (kept at the first line). Two lines with the same column inputs but a different transform are SG208 and neither is applied; keep one.

docs.title: PII and value masking
docs.text: SchemaGuru shows an agent (and a drafting LLM) a few values — the observed values of low-cardinality columns, a handful of examples for others — because "status takes paid, PAID, refunded" is knowledge names cannot give. Personal data in those values is masked by default.

docs.title: Three modes
docs.text:
SamplingConfig.llm_values What leaves SchemaGuru Default masked values, with anything detected as personal replaced by its shape: <email>, <phone>, <name>, <iban>, <card>, <ip>, <uuid>, <secret>, <address>, <hex32> (hex of that length), <free_text len=…> yes raw values unmasked — only on your explicit opt-in no none no values at all: names, types, comments and statistics only no

masked masks values that look personal. A value with no personal shape — an enum code, a filter literal, the maximum of a timestamp column — is shown as it is. If a table's values must not leave in any form, use none: it hides every value and keeps only names, types, comments and counts.

Override per table glob with per_glob — the narrowest matching glob wins, and between equally narrow globs the most restrictive mode wins, so an ambiguous config never widens access:

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.pii import ValuePolicy

cfg = sg.SamplingConfig(per_glob={"shop.*": "masked", "shop.customers": "none"})
for t in ("orders", "customers"):
    print(t, ValuePolicy.for_table(sg.ObjectRef(None, "shop", t), cfg))

Globs match case-insensitively: hr.* covers Snowflake's upper-cased DB.HR.EMPLOYEES as well as hr.employees, because a case-sensitive miss would fail open (the table would fall back to the default mode). A glob that matches no stored table is reported by guru.load_overlays() and schemaguru lint as warning SG507: a typo there would otherwise leave the tables it meant to restrict on the default mode.

Raw samples are written to the store only in raw mode and with store_raw_samples=True (default False).

docs.title: Where masking happens
docs.text:
Values are masked at every boundary, not once:

  • at storage — measured values are stored masked (unless raw is opted into twice, above);
  • in evidence — SQL is stored as a template only, every literal blanked (?);
  • in errors — exception messages are masked before they are recorded or returned;
  • in rendered views — a final shape sweep runs over every view;
  • in every agent tool result, and over every payload sent to a drafting LLM (hits are counted, pii_sweep_hits).

docs.title: Detection: shape first, never name alone
docs.text:
A column is not classified by its name. A frequency enum whose name contains "email" is not an email column; an anonymised identifier that looks like an enum by cardinality is flagged for review rather than auto-classified. Detectors look at values:

from schemaguru.pii import mask_value

for v in ["ann.lee@example.com", "+44 20 7946 0958", "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00",
          "4111 1111 1111 1111", "192.0.2.17", "Ann Lee", "White Paper", "paid"]:
    print(repr(v), "->", mask_value(v))

Shipped detectors: email (including lists), phone (E.164 and national forms), IBAN (checksum), card (Luhn), IPv4/IPv6, UUID, long hex, JWT- and secret-like high-entropy strings, a person-name heuristic, a postal-address heuristic, and free text (over 60 characters with spaces). Blank values count as NULL. Detectors are plug-ins: add one.

  • Hex (<hexN>) is 20 or more hex characters with at least one letter a–f: 16 would mask JSON numbers, and an all-digit run is a number, not a hash.
  • Secrets (<secret>): JWTs, published token shapes (ghp_…, github_pat_…, xoxb-…, xapp-…, AKIA…, sk_live_…, …) even when glued to a word by _ or - (token_ghp_…), the value after a credential key (api_key=…, Bearer …, and quoted forms such as {"token": "…"}, which keep their quotes), and high-entropy strings. After password, passwd or pwd with = or : the value is masked whatever its length (password: hunter2 → password: <secret>, {"password": " x"} → {"password": "<secret>"}), unless it is a column type (password: varchar(255) describes a schema). A path or URL keeps the high-entropy rule on its own text (after the scheme), and is also a secret when a piece of it looks like a token; such a path is masked whole (/var/data/9f86…015/x.csv → <secret>).
  • Addresses (<address>) are masked as whole values and inside sentences: ship to 42 Elm Street, Springfield today → ship to <address> today.

docs.title: The name heuristic, honestly
docs.text:
• Two to four capitalised tokens with at least one hit in the bundled name list are masked as <name>, joined by spaces or a comma (Garcia, Maria, Garcia,Maria), with initials (M. Garcia). This masks some non-names on purpose — product and title terms such as "White Paper", "Brown Sugar" or "Price List" — because failing safe is the point.
  • Two or more listed names in lower case are masked too (maria garcia), and so are some lower-case word pairs that happen to be names ("will mark").
  • A lone listed surname is masked when it is possessive (Garcia's order → <name>'s order).
  • After a person cue — customer, contact, by, from — two to four capitalised tokens are masked even when no token is in the list (customer <name>), and after an honorific (Mr, Ms, Mrs, Dr, Prof, …) one to four are. Prose such as "sorted by Created At" or "Data from Google Analytics" is masked as a result.
  • It does not mask single-token names without a cue (Jean-Luc, a first name alone) or lower-case names outside the list. If such values are personal, use none for that table.
  • Quoted identifiers in stored SQL templates are only masked by shape detectors (email, phone, IBAN, card, IP, UUID, hex, secret), never by the name heuristic, so a column called "Unit Price" survives.

Masking reduces exposure; it is not anonymisation. If a table must not leave your environment in any form, set it to none — or keep it out of the crawl with an exclude glob.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
View definitions read for lineage are not values and never reach a model: the raw SQL is parsed in memory, and only a sha256 and a literal-free template are kept.

Masking trades precision for recall: when a rule cannot tell a personal value from an ordinary one, it masks. What that means in practice:

  • Place and brand names that share a word with the name list are masked as names (Austin Store → <name>): a name list cannot tell a town or a brand from a person.
  • A dotted quad is an IP address whatever precedes it, so a four-part version number is masked (release 2.10.3.1 → release <ip>); three-part and v-prefixed versions (1.2.3, v10.0.1) are kept.
  • A digit string that starts with 00 and a non-zero digit is the international dialling form, so a zero-padded id written that way is masked (0012345678901 → <phone>); ids with three or more leading zeros (000123456) are kept.
  • After password:, passwd: or pwd: any value is masked, a word included (password: required → password: <secret>); only a column type (varchar(255), text, …) is kept, so a password that is literally a type name would show.
  • A path or URL of 24+ varied characters is high-entropy like a token and is masked whole (/data/warehouse/2026/11/25/part-00017-snappy.parquet → <secret>, and so is a long https://… link): a key written in groups (/licenses/AB3X-QZ9K-…) has the same shape.
  • A path or URL holding a random-looking segment is masked whole: a hex or UUID key in a path hides the whole path, not only the key (/var/data/9f86…015/x.csv → <secret>).
  • A quoted credential value runs to its closing quote or the end of the line; an unclosed quote masks the rest of the line.
  • Addresses inside sentences need capitalised street names (42 Elm Street), except before an unambiguous street word (12 baker street); a lower-case 12 baker st inside a sentence is not detected.

docs.title: Refresh and drift
docs.text:
Warehouses move. guru.refresh() (or schemaguru refresh) brings the knowledge up to date and tells you what changed — judged against the previous snapshot, not in absolute terms.

  1. Incremental crawl: new, changed and withdrawn tables (Crawl).
  2. Re-measure facts older than fact_ttl_days (14) and every fact on a changed table, within budget, highest priority first.
  3. Re-check the human and declared expectations on the touched tables.
  4. Snapshot and diff: facts are compared by identity and value, never by timestamp.
  5. Classify each change:
Class Examples BENIGN a measurement moved but kept its verdict; enum values only added; a new non-PII column or table; a key still unique REVIEW a verdict changed; a fact was removed; enum values removed or renamed; a new PII-looking column; a withdrawn table; an expectation newly contradicted; anything unrecognised PRE_EXISTING a contradiction the previous snapshot already had: drift, not a regression of this run NOT_MEASURED a check that did not run this time (budget, error, table not due): never reported as "removed" or "fixed"

A refresh that measured less than the previous one never silently overwrites it: the new snapshot records the checks it ran, and what it could not check is listed as missing.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
first = guru.refresh(label="baseline")
second = guru.refresh(label="nightly")
print(second.exit_code, second.counts())
print(second.to_markdown()[:400])
guru.close()

docs.title: Exit codes for CI
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 nothing needs review 1 at least one REVIEW change 3 errors, or nothing could be measured

report.to_json() and report.to_markdown() give the full report — post the Markdown on a pull request or a chat channel. A typical nightly job:

schemaguru --url "$WAREHOUSE_URL" refresh --label nightly --format markdown > refresh.md

Pair it with view fingerprints to see whether the prompts your agents read changed, and with overlays to turn a recurring finding into a declared expectation (or a waiver with an expiry).

New PII-looking columns are routed to review by name (email, phone, iban, …) — a conservative routing to a person, never a classification: nothing is recorded as PII because of a name. Custom rules: Change classifier.

docs.title: Rendering views
docs.text:
A ContextView is what an agent reads. It is plain text by default, built from ordered blocks, fingerprinted, and rendered the same way every time for the same knowledge.

import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure(all=True)
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")

view = guru.context("refund rate by month")
print(view.tokens, view.fingerprint[:12], [t.canonical() for t in view.tables])
for block in view.blocks:
    print("stable" if block.stable else "scoped", block.text.splitlines()[0])
print(view.to_markdown()[:200])
print(view.to_json()[:200])
print(view.to_xml()[:200])
print(str(guru.context("refund rate by month", format="markdown"))[:80])
  • .text — the default format; str(view) renders the format the view was asked for (format="text" | "markdown" | "json" | "xml", or one you register).
  • .blocks — ordered ViewBlock(stable, text): the blocks that do not depend on the question (global pitfalls, the never-query list) are marked stable and come first, so a host can put a prompt-cache breakpoint after them; the legend, glossary hits and table blocks follow.
  • .tables, .tokens, .fingerprint (SHA-256 of the text), .diagnostics (for example SG505, how many values the value policy masked).

docs.title: Rendering rules
docs.text:
• Consequence order. Warnings come before confirmations, and truncation drops confirmations first, never warnings. A hedge is placed above what it qualifies.
  • Numbers keep their method. measured <date>, verified <date>, ≈ … (sampled f%, …), ≥ … (lower bound); a thin join states its coverage as a number.
  • Drafts are marked (draft); human statements not yet checked are marked (human, unchecked).
  • Values lists are capped (ScopeConfig.max_values_shown, 6) with "+N more".
  • The legend appears only when a ⚠ does, and it always says: absence of a warning is not verification.

docs.title: Fingerprints for CI
docs.text:
guru.fingerprint_views(questions) renders a fixed question set and returns {question: sha256}. Commit it; after a refresh, a changed fingerprint means the prompt your agent reads has changed — review it like code.

prints = guru.fingerprint_views(["refund rate by month", "events per account and session"])
print({q: h[:12] for q, h in prints.items()})
guru.close()

docs.title: Sampling large tables
docs.text: Small tables are measured exactly. A table too large to read in full is measured on a representative sample, and every number from it says so. LIMIT is never a sampling method: it returns rows in storage order and can overstate a rate several times.

docs.title: When a table is large
docs.text:
A table is large when catalog statistics say bytes ≥ sample_threshold_bytes (50 GiB), or, with bytes unknown, row_count ≥ sample_threshold_rows (500M). Everything else is exact.

import schemaguru as sg
from schemaguru.measure import KeyOverlapReq, ProfileColumns, choose_sample, is_large
from schemaguru.model.structure import Table

cfg = sg.SamplingConfig()
big = Table(sg.ObjectRef(None, "shop", "events_raw"), "table", row_count=40_000_000_000,
            bytes=2 << 40)
join = sg.JoinRef((sg.ObjectRef(None, "shop", "events_raw", "session_id"),),
                  (sg.ObjectRef(None, "shop", "sessions", "session_id"),))
print(is_large(big, cfg))
for req in (KeyOverlapReq(join), ProfileColumns(big.ref, ("session_id", "kind"))):
    choice = choose_sample(big, req, cfg, key_distinct=4_000_000_000, est_bytes=big.bytes,
                           max_bytes_per_probe=sg.Budget().max_bytes_per_probe, seed=42)
    print(type(req).__name__, choice.method, choice.fraction)

SamplingConfig(measurement="off") measures everything exactly (probes over budget then become ERROR over_budget); "force" samples every table, for tests and demos.

docs.title: How
docs.text:
Metric Method Why joins (KeyOverlap), uniqueness, fan-out, distinct keys key-hash: keep rows whose hashed key falls in a bucket range all rows of a kept key are kept, so per-key multiplicities are exact; the same hash, seed and range on both sides of a join keep the same keys, so match rate and coverage are unbiased. Used only above exact_key_limit (5M distinct keys), aiming at about that many keys null rates, pattern rates block (SYSTEM) sampling where the dialect has it, else row-level Bernoulli block sampling is what actually cuts bytes billed; its fraction is chosen to fit max_bytes_per_probe (floor 0.1%, ceiling 10%), and intervals are widened by a design effect (2.0) and labelled approximate top values key-hash on the primary key only FactLang reads the input more than once for this probe (FL405), so block samples are refused freshness, row counts, claim verification never sampled a maximum must be exact; row counts come from catalog statistics or an exact count

Two honest costs: on column-billed warehouses (BigQuery) key-hash sampling still scans the key columns in full — cheap, because only key columns are read — and key-hash top values on the primary key do not reduce bytes scanned there, so top values on a huge table can be over budget (SG301).

docs.title: What a sampled number means
docs.text:
• A sampled fact is ESTIMATED, never VERIFIED, and is never compared with an exact one.
  • Ratios carry a Wilson 95% interval: ≈ 3.2% (sampled 1%, ±0.4%).
  • Counts are scaled by 1/fraction and labelled; distinct counts and maxima from a sample are lower bounds (distinct ≥ 377 (sampled 5%, lower bound)).
  • Observed values are "seen in sample"; a rare value the sample missed is not claimed absent.
  • A sampled join's cardinality names only what the sample proved: a side seen repeating a key is N (a repeat is real), a side seen with one row per key is ? (only a lower bound), so N:M, N:? or ?:N; with no repeat on either side it is unknown (cardinality: null, cardinality_reason: "sampled"), never 1:1. A declared 1 side seen repeating still warns.
  • The method string is sampled:<keyhash|system|bernoulli>:<fraction>:<seed>; the seed is fixed per table and snapshot, so re-runs reproduce.

docs.title: A sample can refute, never confirm
docs.text:
A declared enum with an undeclared value seen in the sample is CONTRADICTED (the value exists). A declared-unique key with a duplicate in a key-hash sample is CONTRADICTED. No counter-example in a sample is only ESTIMATED ("consistent with the sample"). For exact confirmation within budget, re-measure the tables behind sampled facts:

facts = guru.store.facts_for([guru.table_ref("events_raw")], None)
exact = guru.verify(facts, exact=True)   # re-measures the sampled tables exactly, if affordable

examples/large_table_sampling.py forces sampling on the small shop tables at 5% so you can see the rendering, intervals and the lower bounds side by side with the true numbers.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text: What SchemaGuru does with a 500,000-table, 25,000,000-column catalog: crawl, incremental crawl, context, join paths and lineage, measured end to end on one machine, with the targets each number is held to, what misses, and how to reproduce it.

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text:
A deterministic synthetic catalog (benchmarks/scale/generator.py, seed 20261125), served page by page by a fake CatalogReader, so nothing ever holds the whole catalog:

  • 500,000 tables, 25,000,000 columns (50 per table) in 100 schemas of 5,000 tables;
  • 50,000 views (every 10th table) with SQL definitions; a view selects from the two tables before it or from the previous view, so lineage chains are up to 6 views deep;
  • two declared foreign keys per non-view table, to lower-numbered tables, and a comment on half of the tables;
  • a MEASURED join fact for every foreign-key pair. These are synthetic: their match rates are a hash of the pair (source: benchmark:synthetic), not measured on any data. Every table ends up in one join component of about 450,000 tables.

The query phases use 200 fixed questions (benchmarks/scale/questions.py), 200 table pairs for join paths and 200 view references for lineage.

docs.title: The machine
docs.text: The committed result (benchmarks/results/0.2.0.json) was run on 2026-11-26 on an Apple M2 Pro, 10 cores, 32 GiB RAM, macOS, Python 3.12.2, runner class local-apple-m2-pro-32g, with nothing else running. Three things were added to the harness's output after the run, and no metric value was edited: the environment.cpu label, re-taken on the same machine with the harness's fixed CPU-model lookup ("arm" became "Apple M2 Pro"); the nightly block; and known_limits[3] and [4] (the measured context_p95_ms and path_p95_ms limits). The whole harness took 54.6 minutes of wall time (3,273 s); the query process peaked at 5.1 GB RSS (the join graph of 900,000 edges).
