Four of the five hard targets pass. The crawl streams: its peak memory (63 MiB) does not grow with the catalog. guru.context p95 misses its target by two orders of magnitude (below). The checks block of the result confirms the run did the work: 500,000 tables written, 50,000 views parsed, 5,000 tables re-read incrementally, and a non-empty answer for all 200 questions, paths and lineage references.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• context latency at 500,000 tables (target missed). p50 9.3 s, p95 28.6 s against a 200 ms target. Profiled at this size, 87% of a call is the join-path search's exact A* lower bound: a reverse Dijkstra over every table within the 6-hop limit of the target, about one second each and about 18 per question (graph expansion's multi-seed searches take 62% of the time, the hazard scan over every pair of candidate tables 34%). In this catalog one join component holds about 450,000 tables, so the 6-hop neighbourhood is a large share of it. The fixes that fit the architecture are in 0.2.0 (below); meeting the target needs an architecture change, such as precomputed distance bounds (landmarks) or a hazard scan that does not search every candidate pair. At 2,000 tables p95 is 119 ms.
  • Join-path search p95 1.2 s (no fixed target; regression-gated): the same per-target bound.
  • The join facts are synthetic (hash-derived rates); a view's declared columns are not derived from its definition; context runs against a store with no column-level facts beyond the crawl. A real catalog with a sparser join graph does less path-search work.

docs.title: Fixed in 0.2.0 by this benchmark
docs.text:
• context read and re-verified every JOIN fact in the store on every call; it now reads a table's joins by subject through an index built with the join graph (every fact read is still id-verified). At 2,000 tables p95 went from 259 ms to 119 ms.
  • The path search's lower bound walked the whole join component per target; it now stops at the hop limit, with identical routes. With the join read above, context at 20,000 tables went from p50 3.9 s / p95 5.3 s to p50 1.0 s / p95 1.5 s.
  • The crawl re-read every lineage fact for every re-parsed view (an index the query planner did not use): quadratic in views, 105 s of lineage at 100,000 tables. It is now linear (124 s at 500,000).
  • refresh compared the two snapshots twice; the Postgres store read every glossary term for every crawled page.

docs.title: Nightly regression workflow
docs.text:
.github/workflows/bench.yml runs at 03:17 UTC and on workflow_dispatch, never on a push or pull request, and is not a required check. It runs the harness at 500,000 tables on ubuntu-latest (runner class github-ubuntu-latest, 350-minute budget), compares the result, and uploads bench.json whatever the outcome.

Why 500,000: projected from the run above with 30% headroom, the store needs 9.48 GB on disk (12.3 GB of the runner's ~14 GB, the tightest limit), the query process 5.1 GB of RAM (6.7 of 16 GiB), and 54.6 minutes here becomes about 109 minutes on a runner core assumed half as fast (142 of 350 with headroom). This is a projection; the first dispatched run confirms it.

The comparator fails the job when a hard target is missed or a regression-gated metric is more than 25% worse than the committed baseline for the same runner class and size. A hard-target miss whose metric a known_limits entry names (here context_p95_ms, with its measured numbers) is reported as a warning instead of a failure, and that metric is then regression-gated at 25% like the others, so the documented miss cannot get worse unnoticed; a miss no known limit names still fails. The entry may be in the result itself or in a committed result at the same table count, from any machine: a nightly result documents no limits, 0.2.0.json does. The GitHub baseline (benchmarks/results/baseline-github-ubuntu-latest.json) is the first workflow_dispatch run on 2026-11-26 (context p95 45.6 s, about 1.6x the M2 Pro figure); with no baseline for the runner class and size the comparator exits 2 ("gate inactive"), which the workflow reports as a warning, not a failure.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python3 -m benchmarks.scale.harness --tables 500000 --out bench.json \
    --runner-class local-<your-machine> --workdir <a directory with 15 GB free>
python3 -m benchmarks.scale.compare bench.json --baseline-dir benchmarks/results

--tables 20000 takes a few minutes. The comparator exits 0 (pass; a known-limit miss is a warning), 1 (a missed target no known limit names, or a regression), 2 (no baseline for this runner class and size: hard targets checked, regressions not) or 3 (not a result file). pytest -m benchmark tests/unit/benchmarks runs a 2,000-table version.

See also: Cost and scale, Join graph and path search, Scoping.

docs.title: Scoping
docs.text: A warehouse with 100,000 tables does not fit in a prompt, and dumping the schema is the wrong default even when it does. guru.context(question, budget_tokens=4000) picks the slice a question needs and fits it into the budget.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
1. Seeds. The retriever ranks tables for the question (ScopeConfig.seed_k, 8). The default LexicalRetriever is the store's full-text search (SQLite FTS5, BM25) over name tokens (snake_case and camelCase split), column names, comments, descriptions, use cases, pitfalls and the glossary terms mapped to the table, plus a boost for a table named verbatim in the question (shop.orders or orders).
  2. Glossary. A glossary term or metric whose words all occur in the question pulls in its mapped tables.
  3. Bridges. The best measured join path between each pair of seeds is added, at most max_expansion_tables (6) extra tables, so the agent sees the tables that connect its seeds — and the refusals between them.
  4. Fit. Tables are ranked (seed score, then bridges) and each is rendered at the richest detail level that still fits: full → standard → lite (columns by priority: keys, join columns, columns named by pitfalls or soft-delete rules, columns with descriptions or values, then the rest) → name-only. Warnings are kept before confirmations at every level.
  5. Always-on blocks. Global pitfalls, the never-query list and the legend, within budget.
  6. The view ends with a "Not shown" line counting the other candidate tables, and the agent tools (search_tables, describe_table) fetch more when needed.
import schemaguru as sg

guru = sg.Guru.connect("duckdb:///warehouse.duckdb")
guru.measure(all=True)
guru.load_overlays("schemaguru.yaml")
for budget in (4000, 600, 250):
    view = guru.context("revenue per customer from paid orders", budget_tokens=budget)
    print(budget, "->", view.tokens, "tokens,", [t.table for t in view.tables])
print(guru.context("which active customer ordered", budget_tokens=600).text[-300:])

When even the always-on blocks do not fit, the view says so (SG504) rather than silently dropping a warning. Tokens are counted by a pluggable counter: the default is a characters-divided-by-four heuristic; Config(token_counter="tiktoken") (extra tiktoken) counts real tokens, or pass token_counter= to Guru (extending).

docs.title: Deterministic and cached
docs.text:
The same store snapshot, question and configuration render a byte-identical view; table order never depends on dict order or timing. Views are cached in an LRU (ScopeConfig.cache_entries, 256) keyed on the snapshot, the question, the configuration and the day; every write through the Guru invalidates the cache.

a = guru.context("refund rate by month")
b = guru.context("refund rate by month")
print(a.fingerprint == b.fingerprint, a.fingerprint[:16])
guru.close()

docs.title: Scale
docs.text: Search runs inside the store (the FTS index), never as a Python scan over every table: on a synthetic 500,000-table store the search p95 was about 167 ms on the developer's machine (hardware-dependent); the whole context call at that size is far slower (p95 28.6 s, a documented known limit, see Scale). If the local SQLite lacks FTS5, search falls back to a slower LIKE scan with a warning (SG701). The join graph is built from the store's join facts and cached until the knowledge changes.

docs.title: Other retrievers
docs.text: HybridRetriever(*retrievers) fuses rankings by reciprocal rank; EmbeddingRetriever(store, embedder) (extra embeddings) ranks by cosine similarity with a pluggable Embedder. Pass one as Guru(retriever=...); see Retriever and embedder.

docs.title: First touch
docs.text: A scoped table that was never measured is marked unmeasured in the view and queued for measurement; the view is not blocked on it unless measure_on_demand="block" (capped by block_timeout_s). See Measure.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: What SchemaGuru touches, what it stores, what it sends, and where its protections end.

docs.title: Read-only by construction
docs.text:
• SchemaGuru never writes to a warehouse. Catalog readers run metadata SELECT/SHOW statements on system views, with a bind parameter for every value; that metadata SQL is the only SQL SchemaGuru authors. Measurement SQL is rendered and run by FactLang.
  • DuckDB files are opened read-only; a mistyped path is an error, not a new file.
  • Give SchemaGuru a warehouse role that can read the system catalog and the data it should measure, and nothing more. Measurement cost is bounded by the budget.

docs.title: What the store holds
docs.text: The store (one SQLite file by default, or Postgres) holds structure, facts and a budget ledger. In the default masked mode, observed values are stored with personal data replaced by its shape; raw values are stored only with llm_values="raw" and store_raw_samples=True. Evidence keeps SQL as a template with every literal blanked. Runtime feedback stores identifiers and counts, never SQL text. Treat the store like the catalog it mirrors: it reveals table and column names, statistics and low-cardinality values.

docs.title: What leaves
docs.text:
• To an agent: views and tool results, after the value policy, a final shape sweep and free-text masking (PII).
  • To an LLM (only when you run drafting): table and column metadata, measured statistics and values under the same policy; every payload is swept in masked mode. Use none for tables whose values must never leave.
  • In errors and logs: connection URLs are shown as scheme://host only — never user, password, path or query; a URL that does not parse cleanly is shown as scheme://***. Driver error messages are scrubbed of embedded URLs.

docs.title: Spending on an agent's behalf
docs.text: An agent's question never spends warehouse money by itself (measure_on_demand="queue"). check_fact, the one agent tool that runs on the warehouse, is off by default (agent_checks="deny"); with "allow" each call is priced and admitted through the budget.

docs.title: The read-only guard helper
docs.text:
SchemaGuru does not execute agent SQL. If your host does, sg.guard.check_sql is a best-effort pre-check — a deny-list helper, not a sandbox:

import schemaguru as sg

never = [sg.ObjectRef(None, "shop", "orders_backup_2019")]
for sql in [
    "SELECT count(*) FROM shop.orders WHERE status = 'paid'",
    "SELECT email FROM shop.customers WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com'",
    "DELETE FROM shop.orders",
    "SELECT 1; DROP TABLE shop.orders",
    "SELECT * FROM read_csv('/etc/passwd')",
    "SELECT * FROM shop.orders_backup_2019",
]:
    verdict = sg.guard.check_sql(sql, "duckdb", never_query=never)
    print(verdict.ok, verdict.reasons)

It requires a single statement starting with SELECT or WITH, applies a DML/DDL keyword deny-list after removing comments and string literals (so '%@x.y' does not trigger it), caps the length, and refuses never-query tables. It also refuses, fail-safe:

  • SQL whose string or comment structure differs between dialects — so # comments, $$ strings, bracketed identifiers containing quotes, and triple quotes may be refused;
  • functions that run SQL from text or read files, file-as-table string literals and path-like quoted identifiers (/, or a file suffix such as .csv, .parquet, .avro, .orc, .gz, .bz2) in any FROM/JOIN position, on any part of a qualified name (s."x.csv");
  • a few legitimate forms it cannot tell apart from the above: substring(x FROM 'regex'), ARRAY['a', 'b'], x['key'].

Run agent SQL under a read-only warehouse role. The guard catches mistakes; permissions stop adversaries.

docs.title: Never-query tables
docs.text: never_query in an overlay lists tables agents must not use; every view states the list and the guard refuses SQL reading them when you pass it. This works against a cooperative agent. Isolation from an adversarial one is the warehouse's job: do not grant the role access to those tables.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• On hosts that take SQL text only (execute(sql)), for the backtick dialects (MySQL, BigQuery, Databricks) a probe whose identifier contains #, // or -- is refused (SG104), because some of those dialects read them as comments. The metadata guard likewise refuses PostgreSQL's #> / # operators and DuckDB's // operator in code; no shipped traffic sends them.
  • View definitions are read for lineage through the same metadata guard (catalog views only, never a data table). The raw text stays in memory while it is parsed; the store keeps a sha256 and a literal-free template, and nothing raw is logged, rendered, put in a diagnostic or sent to an LLM.
  • The metadata guard refuses a ; inside a backtick identifier (`a;b`), as FactLang's own metadata guard does: where backticks are not identifier quotes (Postgres, the ANSI default) that ; separates statements. Plain backtick and bracket identifiers (`table_name`, [table_name]) pass.
  • A text value holding a backtick cannot be inlined on hosts that take SQL text only (SG109, refused fail-safe because some dialects read a backtick as an identifier quote); pass a DB-API connection or an engine for bound parameters.
  • literal_refusal in schemaguru.catalog.executor is a public name since 0.1.1 and stays under that name: renaming it would remove a released name. It returns a specific reason a rendered literal is refused (today the zone-less Databricks timestamp), or None.

docs.text: Bearer tokens of at least 16 characters, compared in constant time, never logged or echoed; roles reader and admin; localhost binding by default; internal errors are logged, not returned. See Server mode.

docs.title: Server mode
docs.text:
The library needs no service. When a team wants one shared knowledge store behind HTTP — several agents, several replicas — schemaguru serve (extra server: Starlette and uvicorn) exposes the same operations as the Python API. The server is a thin layer: every route calls a public Guru method or handle_tool_call, so there is no logic that only the server has.

pip install 'schemaguru[server,postgres-store]'
export SCHEMAGURU_SERVER_TOKENS="$ADMIN_TOKEN:admin,$READER_TOKEN:reader"
schemaguru --store postgresql://sg@db/knowledge --url "$WAREHOUSE_URL" serve --port 8080

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Route Calls Role GET /healthz liveness; the only route without a token — POST /context Guru.context (JSON question, budget_tokens, profile, format) reader GET /search?q=&k= search_tables reader GET /tables/{ref} describe_table reader GET /paths?from=&to= find_join_path reader GET /lineage?ref=&direction=&depth=&level= lineage (guide); a custom store without the lineage index answers SG705 (HTTP 501) reader GET /facts?subject=&kind= stored facts of one subject, masked by the tool surface's value policy reader POST /refresh Guru.refresh (JSON label), one at a time admin /mcp MCP over streamable HTTP (the same tools and schema://tables/{ref} resources as schemaguru mcp; JSON responses, stateful sessions); 501 (SG812) without the mcp extra reader

Errors are JSON {"error": {"code": "SG8xx", "message": …}}: a missing or invalid token is 401 (SG805), a reader on an admin route 403 (SG806), a bad request 400 (SG807), an unknown table 404 (SG808), a refresh already running 409 (SG809), anything unexpected 500 (SG810, details logged, never returned).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
v1 uses bearer tokens mapped to a role, reader or admin: from tokens= or the SCHEMAGURU_SERVER_TOKENS environment variable (token:role,…; a token without a role is a reader). Tokens must be at least 16 characters, are compared in constant time and are never logged or echoed. With no usable token the server refuses to start (SG811). It binds to 127.0.0.1 unless you pass --host. Bring your own scheme with an Authenticator.

from schemaguru.server import BearerTokens, create_app, serve

app = create_app(guru, authenticator=BearerTokens({"a-long-reader-token": "reader"}))  # ASGI
serve(guru, host="0.0.0.0", port=8080, tokens={"a-long-admin-token-123": "admin"})

docs.title: Sharing a store
docs.text:
--store postgres://… (extra postgres-store) opens a PostgresStore: the same schema as the SQLite store, with weighted tsvector full-text search. Several replicas can share it; refresh holds a Postgres advisory lock (pg_try_advisory_lock), so only one replica refreshes at a time and the others get 409. With a SQLite store a process lock does the same within one process.

Overlay rules (waypoints, chains, waivers) live on the Guru object; to serve them, build the Guru in Python, load the overlays, and pass it to create_app or serve.
